The Crest–Root Calculus

A graded estimator calculus joining point counts, central zeros, Mordell–Weil lattices and height growth, from curves to tenfolds, with a numerical program run to \(x = 10^{7}\)

Canonical edition · 22 November 2026

Parts I–XXX are integrated through §148. The public edition has a separate publication history.

Part XXX. Sections 138–143 give a certified single-prime decision procedure for cubic elliptic quotients. Sections 144–147 classify Fermat reductions, determine degree spectra, and recover the contact points of nonsplit quartic twists.

Important corrections: The early \(2/\pi\) spectral-law fit was largely tautological and withdrawn; the original excised-ensemble normalization was reversed; the initial Part XIX contact count was six valid conics, not eight; benchmark recoveries contained duplicate curves; statistical Conjectures E and F were not supported in their original forms. Previous theorem text is retained for historical traceability with inline revisions.

Open questions. Practical costs for general large-field scans and rational origins on arbitrary genus-one quotients remain open, alongside the earlier questions on global GRH, rank-four central multiplicities and zeta spectra of the cubic tower.

The accompanying research release includes the exact proof receipts, original and revised evidence, updated 57-item work register and source SHA-256 inventory.

AbstractI build one formalism that reads a smooth projective variety \(X/\Q\), or a self-dual motive \(M\), through two dual data. The root is the sequence of local point counts \(N_p(X)\). The crest is the family of growth exponents and constants that this sequence forces on global objects: partial Euler products, prime sums normalized at the centre, lattice-point counts in the Mordell–Weil lattice, and rational-point counts of bounded height. The calculus is graded. The order-one crest \(\kk^{(j)}\) reads the Galois-invariant rank of \(H^{2j}\) through a balanced base-\(p\) expansion of \(N_p\). The central crest reads the order of vanishing at the centre through a crest mean \(\mathfrak M\), a crest variance \(\mathfrak V\) and a crest budget \(\mathfrak B\). These are tied by closed-form identities whose right-hand sides are computable from the conductor and one absolutely convergent prime sum. The height crest reads the same integers back off lattice and height counting. The program evaluates every identity numerically: five elliptic curves of rank 0 to 4 to \(x = 10^{7}\), symmetric squares and cubes, diagonal quadrics in \(\mathbb P^{1}\) through \(\mathbb P^{10}\), diagonal cubics in \(\mathbb P^{2}\) through \(\mathbb P^{5}\), saturated Mordell–Weil lattices, and Manin counting on \(\mathbb P^{1}\times\mathbb P^{1}\) to \(B = 10^{6}\). Every identity closes within its predicted finite-window error. Section 9 sets out four conjectures, labelled by how strong the evidence for each is. Part II (§§11–13) certifies the crest statistics in interval arithmetic to \(x=10^{8}\). It also tests the uncertainty conjecture on 492 quadratic twists up to conductor \(10^{8}\). That test refutes the conjecture's original \((\log N)^2\) form. Part III (§§14–16) responds to an external audit. It corrects a factor in the Manin count, makes the point counter provably exact, states the conditional status of the zero lists, and withdraws the lowest-zero "law" of §12 as largely definitional, keeping only its complexity consequence and a sharper question about the residual. Part IV (§§17–19) answers that question. The excised orthogonal ensemble fits the lowest zero but is rejected out of sample (p down to 0.003). The residual turns out to be arithmetic: \(\chi_d(2),\chi_d(3),\chi_d(5)\) explain about two-thirds of its variance. Part V (§§20–23) builds a certified spectral calculator that uses no zero list. Starting from the parallel session's resolvent identity, it delivers \(\mathfrak D_E\) to 31–36 certified digits on all five curves. It also gives two-sided \(\gamma_1\) enclosures, certified first zeros, and certified complete zero lists up to heights between 9 and 34. Part VI (§§24–27) certifies the budget to about 72 digits by two independent algorithms, recomputes the analytic inputs by an independent method, and adds an exact-rational certificate checker that rejects forgeries. It also reruns 39 twists entirely on certified inputs, all 39 consistent with the dataset. Part VII (§§28–31) removes PARI from the trusted base with a pure-Python arithmetic checker, and certifies all 122 twists with \(|d|\le200\). On those certified, non-circular inputs, the primes 2, 3 and 5 explain 85% of the rank-0 residual. Part VIII (§§32–36) adds a native FLINT calculator with deflated quadrature and certifies the entire 492-twist family in 97 CPU-minutes. It derives the law from the identity \(\mathfrak D=(\mathfrak B-r)+\mathcal E\), whose predicted per-prime shape is confirmed. It also runs the first class-conditional test of Conjecture E: the excision cutoff shifts as predicted, but the held-out spacing fails. Part IX (§§37–40) checks the parallel session's Part IX and confirms its correction to my ensemble unfolding. It reruns the whole family through hash-bound native code, so that all 492 certificates pass a three-link chain: independent coefficient hash, consumed-input hash, and exact-rational deduction check. With the corrected unfolding, Conjecture E is refuted in every form tested. Part X (§§41–44) adds a second rigorous algorithm, panelled Gauss–Legendre quadrature in Arb. All 492 certificates rebuilt from it alone pass the exact-rational audit, giving two independent chains. It also corrects the PIT for atomic statistics. With that correction, a conditional high-spectrum model becomes the first to predict the low-lying residual out of sample (Conjecture F). Part XI (§§45–48) builds certified transfer families of twists of 37a1 and 389a1, with rank 0 certified directly. It confirms Waldspurger squareness on 516 certified central values. On exact certified features, Conjecture F is refuted and the §43 success is withdrawn as an interpolation artifact. Part XII (§§49–51) checks the parallel session's exact three-point completion theorem and generalizes it to an exact \(k\)-point Farkas certificate with Sturm verification. With eight points, the first zero is localized to about \(10^{-6}\) relative and the second to about \(10^{-4}\), from positivity alone. Part XIII (§§52–55) reproduces the quantization hierarchy and adds unconditional zero counts by rigorous Taylor-model contours. These prove GRH and list completeness for 11a1 up to height 27.76 and for 37a1 up to 32.74, and make the low spectra of all 501 twists GRH-free. Part XIV (§§56–62) raises the contour certificates to heights 40–100, proving GRH and simplicity for 11a1 and 37a1 up to height 100 with no input from earlier certificates. It runs the quantization hierarchy on the tail after complete removal of the proven spectrum and calibrates it: the hierarchy detects bookkeeping and mass errors but is blind to off-line zeros. It checks the parallel session's Spectral Foundry by two independent routes and proves that trace width bounds the smoothness of the Jacobian group. Finally it constructs a genus-37 curve with prescribed local zeta functions at 3 and 5 and certified Mordell–Weil rank at least 12. Part XV (§§63–66) checks the parallel session's hidden-motive engine, whose computations all reproduce. It explains the collapse of 163 constructions to 60 spectra by the translation \(x\mapsto x+1\), up to one accident, and a twist law for \(PGL_2(\mathbb F_3)\). It shows the residual isogeny relations are forced by a 34-factor alphabet. It also carries out the proposed global correspondence synthesis. For the genus-37 covers over \(\mathbb Q\), local coprimality at primes below 20 certifies that the global idempotent lattice is generated by the 15 automorphism projectors, and that 7 of the 9 local projectors at 3 cannot lift. Part XVI (§§67–71) checks the parallel session's automorphism-free quartic with an independent counter. It proves the split and inert laws of real multiplication defined over \(K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_9)^+\) and confirms them in all 50 good cases, with \(a_1=a_2=0\) at every inert prime. It shows \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\), so the hidden structure lives only over \(K\). For the cover quotient \(B=D/\tau\) it proves \(\operatorname{End}^0_K(\operatorname{Jac}B)=K\), by an explicit correspondence whose action on \(H^1\) yields the Frobenius elements \(t_p\in\mathcal O_K\). \(B\) matches the quartic in all 27 exact point counts. Part XVII (§§72–75) proves the parallel session's explicit isomorphism \(D_t/\tau\cong C_u\) independently for generic \(t\), which makes \(\operatorname{End}^0_K(\operatorname{Jac}C)=K\) unconditional. It verifies an automorphism-free quartic whose Jacobian splits as \(E\times A\) through a degree-3 map, with \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\overline{\mathbb Q}}(A)=\mathbb Q\) certified at 9 primes. It also recovers the elliptic factor from zeta data alone, without being told \(E\). Part XVIII (§§76–79) confirms the parallel session's map-discovery identities and its Cartier recovery, at all 12 good primes up to 59. It shows that its search depends on the choice of coordinates, finding 1 of 8 curves after projective changes. It explains the pencil intrinsically, through the fibre over \(O_E\) and the totally tangent conics over 2-torsion, and replaces the search with one that is invariant under projective changes. That search recovers 8 of 8 with no false positives on the negative controls. Part XIX (§§80–83) removes the line-height search entirely for this genus-three subcover family: it solves the totally tangent conic equations modulo suitable primes, Hensel-lifts an incidence line, and recovers the degree-three elliptic morphism by exact square completion. It succeeds on all 12 projectively scrambled reference curves, nine distinct family targets, and eight scrambled family members, with exact independent map certificates and explicit limitations at nonsplit contact primes. Part XX (§§84–88) checks Part XIX with independent code and corrects two of its counts. It then proves that every degree-three elliptic subcover of a smooth plane quartic has exactly two collinear fibres, whose residual points are the only possible base points. It also proves that the square-completion criterion is necessary as well as sufficient, with affine lower coefficients forced by Riemann–Roch. That replaces the modular search, splitting condition and Hensel lifting with an exact elimination in four unknowns. On \(C^\star\) the elimination finds the second base point \((-3{:}1{:}0)\), which Part XIX never tested. In all 13 frames it returns exactly one pencil at each base point and none at the third rational point, and for \(C^\star\) that count is proved by theory.

Epistemic labelsThroughout, Theorem marks a classical result cited, not reproved. Derived marks a statement I derive here from stated hypotheses, usually GRH plus linear independence of zero ordinates (LI). Measured marks a number produced by the accompanying code. Conjecture marks a proposal I put forward. To be blunt about scope: no part of this program proves the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, the Riemann hypothesis for any \(L\)-function, or the Tate conjecture. What it does is recast each of them as an estimator identity with an explicit target, testable from point counts alone. Every number on this page is something the code can falsify. The individual ingredients (Mertens, Chebotarev, the explicit formula, Hadamard factorisation, Goldfeld's partial-product theorem, Manin's conjecture, BSD) are classical. What is new is that they are assembled into one graded calculus, together with the variance and budget identities used as rank estimators, the graded symmetry-offset law, the crest form of BSD, the compressed exact counting algorithm, and the dimension ladder.

1. The root datum and its balanced expansion

Let \(X\) be smooth, projective and geometrically integral of dimension \(d\) over \(\Q\), with good reduction outside a finite set \(S\). For \(p \notin S\), let \(N_p = \#X(\F_p)\). By the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula, \(N_p = \sum_{i=0}^{2d}(-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(\Frob_p \mid H^i_{\text{ét}}(X_{\bar\Q},\Q_\ell))\). By Deligne, every eigenvalue on \(H^i\) has absolute value \(p^{i/2}\). The root datum of \(X\) is the function \(\mathcal R_X : p \mapsto N_p\). Here \(p\) is a rational prime and \(N_p\) a non-negative integer, so the root datum is just a sequence of integers indexed by primes.

The first new device is the balanced expansion. Write \[ N_p = \sum_{j=0}^{d} \lambda_j(p)\, p^{j}, \qquad \lambda_j(p) \in \Z,\quad |\lambda_j(p)| \le \tfrac{p-1}{2}, \] which exists and is unique for every integer, since it is base-\(p\) notation with digits centred at zero. In general the digits \(\lambda_j(p)\) mean nothing. In the Tate regime they mean a great deal. In that regime the odd cohomology vanishes and every eigenvalue of \(\Frob_p\) on \(H^{2j}\) has the form \(\zeta p^{j}\) with \(\zeta\) a root of unity. Then \(\operatorname{tr}(\Frob_p\mid H^{2j}) = t_j(p)\, p^{j}\) with \(t_j(p)\) an algebraic integer of absolute value at most \(b_{2j} = \dim H^{2j}\). Once \(p > 2\max_j b_{2j}+1\) and the traces are rational, the digit \(\lambda_j(p)\) equals \(t_j(p)\) exactly. So the balanced expansion splits the single integer \(N_p\) into the Frobenius traces of each cohomological degree, without computing any cohomology.

Definition 1.1The graded crest of \(X\) is the vector \(\kk(X) = (\kk^{(0)},\dots,\kk^{(d)})\), where \[ \kk^{(j)}(X) = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{\pi(x)} \sum_{p\le x,\ p\notin S} \lambda_j(p). \] Here \(\pi(x)\) is the prime-counting function, so \(\kk^{(j)}\) is the natural-density average of the \(j\)-th balanced digit over primes.

Theorem(Chebotarev, Weil.) In the Tate regime, the Galois action on \(H^{2j}(j)\) factors through a finite group \(G_j\). The trace average over Frobenius classes, weighted by Chebotarev density, equals the dimension of the \(G_j\)-invariants. So \(\kk^{(j)}(X) = \dim H^{2j}(X_{\bar\Q},\Q_\ell(j))^{\mathrm{Gal}}\), the rank of the Tate classes of codimension \(j\) defined over \(\Q\). By the Tate conjecture, which is known in all the cases treated below, this is the rank of the group of codimension-\(j\) algebraic cycles over \(\Q\) modulo homological equivalence. In particular \(\kk^{(1)}(X) = \rho(X)\), the Picard rank over \(\Q\).

The calculus side is Mertens' theorem. Since \(N_p/p^{d} = 1 + \lambda_{d-1}(p)/p + O(p^{-2})\) in the Tate regime, and \(\sum_{p\le x}1/p = \log\log x + M_0 + o(1)\), we get \[ \prod_{p\le x} \frac{N_p}{p^{d}} \sim \mathfrak c_X\,(\log x)^{\kk^{(d-1)}(X)}, \] where \(\kk^{(d-1)} = \kk^{(1)} = \rho\) by Poincaré duality. The partial Euler product of normalized counts therefore grows like a power of \(\log x\), and the exponent is the Picard rank. This is the order-one crest. Its convergence factor \(\prod_p(1-p^{-1})^{\rho} N_p/p^{d}\) is exactly the Euler product in Peyre's constant for Manin's conjecture. That is the first sign that a crest exponent controls height growth.

2. Exact counting by orbit compression

To evaluate \(\kk\) across dimensions, I count points on diagonal hypersurfaces \(X_{e,k} : \sum_{i=1}^{k} c_i x_i^{e} = 0\) in \(\mathbb P^{k-1}\) exactly, with arbitrary-precision integers. The method is the second device: a cyclotomic class algebra. Let \(g = \gcd(e,p-1)\) and let \(r\) be a primitive root mod \(p\). Partition \(\F_p\) into the zero class \(C_\ast = \{0\}\) and the \(g\) cosets \(C_i = \{r^{i+g m}\}\) of the subgroup of \(e\)-th powers. Here \(i\) runs over \(\Z/g\) and \(m\) over integers. The value \(c x^{e}\), for \(x\) ranging over \(\F_p\), lands in \(C_\ast\) once and in the single coset containing \(c\) exactly \(p-1\) times. The distribution of a partial sum over these \(g+1\) classes evolves under addition through the structure constants \[ \sigma_{ij}^{\,\ell} = \#\{(a,b) \in C_i\times C_j : a+b \in C_\ell\}, \] which are the classical cyclotomic numbers of order \(g\). I compute each \(\sigma_{ij}\) once per prime by exact int64 direct convolution of class indicators, folded mod \(p\). The first edition used a rounded floating-point FFT, which is exact in practice but not provably so; see §14. Every later step multiplies exact integer vectors of length \(g+1\). The affine count \(A_p = \#\{x\in\F_p^{k} : \sum c_i x_i^{e}=0\}\) is the \(C_\ast\)-component after \(k\) steps, and \(N_p = (A_p-1)/(p-1)\). The cost is \(O(g^2p^2 + k g^{3})\) per prime instead of \(O(p^{k})\), and there is no floating-point error in any count. The code checks itself by brute force at \(p \in \{5,7,11,13\}\) for \((e,k) \in \{(2,4),(3,4),(2,5)\}\), and it applies those assertions before every run.

The structure is exact. For even \(d = k-2\), the middle trace is \(p^{d/2}(1+\varepsilon_p)\), where \(\varepsilon_p = \big(\tfrac{(-1)^{k/2}}{p}\big)\) is the Legendre symbol of the signed discriminant. When \(k\equiv 0 \pmod 4\), the signed discriminant \((-1)^{k/2}\) equals \(+1\), so \(\varepsilon_p = 1\) for every \(p\): both rulings of the middle-dimensional linear spaces are defined over \(\Q\), and \(\kk^{(d/2)} = 2\). When \(k \equiv 2 \pmod 4\), \(\varepsilon_p = \big(\tfrac{-1}{p}\big)\) averages to zero, the two rulings are swapped by \(\mathrm{Gal}(\Q(i)/\Q)\), and \(\kk^{(d/2)} = 1\). The measured \(0.9789\) is \(1 + (\pi_{1(4)} - \pi_{3(4)})/\pi\) on the sample. That is Chebyshev's bias between primes \(\equiv 1\) and \(\equiv 3 \pmod 4\), visible in a crest digit. The case \(k=4\) is the split quadric \(\cong \mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\), whose Picard rank is 2. Arithmetically this is the factorisation of the quaternion norm. The periodicity \(k \bmod 4\) of the middle crest of \(\Z^{k}\) matches the classical fact that \(r_4\) and \(r_8\) are pure divisor sums: Jacobi's formulas, coming from the multiplicative norm forms of the quaternions and octonions. The crest exposes this periodicity as an integer jump in one Galois-invariant rank.

MeasuredThe diagonal cubics \(F_k : \sum_{i\le k} x_i^{3} = 0\) climb into the non-Tate regime. Here the crest separates algebraic structure from transcendental oscillation. For \(p \equiv 2 \pmod 3\), cubing is a bijection of \(\F_p\), so \(N_p\) equals the count of a hyperplane and every primitive trace vanishes. For \(p\equiv 1 \pmod 3\), let \(\tau_p = (N_p - \sum_{j=0}^{d} p^{j})/p^{d/2}\) be the normalized primitive middle trace. The measured values over primes \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 3\) below 1500 are as follows. On the cubic curve \(F_3\), which is the CM elliptic curve of conductor 27, \(\tau\) has mean \(-0.083\) and second moment \(1.963\), against the Sato–Tate–Hecke value 2 for \(|2\cos\theta|^2\). On the cubic surface \(F_4\), \(\tau_p = 6\) exactly at every split prime, so the mean of \(\tau\) over all primes is \(3\) and \(\rho(F_4/\Q) = 1+3 = 4\): six primitive classes over \(\Q(\zeta_3)\), averaged against conjugation. On the cubic threefold \(F_5\), \(\tau\) has mean \(-0.42\), consistent with zero, and second moment \(49.07\). That matches \(2m^2\) with \(m=5\), which says the primitive \(H^3\) is \(5\)-isotypic for a single weight-one CM Hecke character, as an intermediate Jacobian isogenous to the fifth power of the \(j=0\) curve requires. On the cubic fourfold \(F_6\), \(\tau\) has mean \(19.963\) and second moment \(400.46\) at split primes. That decomposes as \(20 + 2\cos\theta_p\), with residual second moment \(1.94\) against the predicted 2. So 20 primitive Tate classes are visible over \(\Q(\zeta_3)\), 10 are invariant over \(\Q\), and with the hyperplane class \(\kk^{(2)}(F_6/\Q) = 11\). The two transcendental classes, which carry \(h^{3,1}\) and \(h^{1,3}\), equidistribute. This is the "multiplicity readout" property of the calculus: second moments of normalized traces count isotypic multiplicities squared, with no cohomology computed.

4. The central crest: odd weight and the centre

For a curve of genus one the order-one crest is blind: \(N_p/p = 1 + (1-a_p)/p\) with \(a_p = p+1-N_p\), and the average of \(1-a_p\) is 1 whatever the rank. The rank lives one order deeper, at the centre of the functional equation, where convergence is only conditional. I set up the central crest for an elliptic curve \(E/\Q\) of conductor \(N\). By modularity its \(L\)-function \(L(E,s) = \prod_{p}L_p(E,s)\) continues to \(\mathbb C\). The completion \(\Lambda(E,s) = N^{s/2}(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s)L(E,s)\) satisfies \(\Lambda(E,s) = w_E\Lambda(E,2-s)\) with root number \(w_E \in \{\pm1\}\). The centre is \(s=1\). Write \(r\) for the order of vanishing there and the nontrivial zeros as \(1+i\gamma\), with \(\gamma \in \R\) under GRH. Write \(a_p = \alpha_p+\beta_p\), \(\alpha_p\beta_p = p\), and \(\Lambda_E(p^k) = (\alpha_p^k+\beta_p^k)\log p\), so that \(-L'/L(E,s) = \sum_n \Lambda_E(n)n^{-s}\).

Definition 4.1The central crest function is \[ T_E(x) = \frac{1}{x}\sum_{p\le x} a_p \log p, \] studied as a function of \(u = \log x\). Fix a window \(u\in[u_0,u_0+U]\), with \(u_0\) the start and \(U\) the length. The crest mean is \(\mathfrak M_E(U) = U^{-1}\int T_E(e^u)\,du\), and the crest variance is \(\mathfrak V_E(U) = U^{-1}\int (T_E(e^u)-\mathfrak M_E)^2\,du\). The crest budget is \[ \mathfrak B_E = \operatorname{Re}\frac{\Lambda'}{\Lambda}(E,2) = \tfrac12\log N - \log 2\pi + (1-\gamma_{\mathrm E}) + \frac{L'}{L}(E,2), \] with \(\gamma_{\mathrm E}\) Euler's constant and \(1-\gamma_{\mathrm E} = \psi(2)\) the digamma value. The term \(\tfrac{L'}{L}(E,2) = -\sum_n \Lambda_E(n) n^{-2}\) converges absolutely, so \(\mathfrak B_E\) can be computed from the root datum and the conductor alone.

Derived(Crest mean law.) The truncated explicit formula gives \(\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda_E(n) = -\sum_{\rho} x^{\rho}/\rho + O(\log^{2}(Nx))\). Here the sum runs over all zeros \(\rho\), counted with multiplicity and taken symmetrically. The zero at \(\rho=1\) contributes \(-r x\). The prime squares contribute \(\sum_{p\le\sqrt x}(a_p^2-2p)\log p\). Rankin–Selberg theory for \(\mathrm{Sym}^2 E\), which has no pole at the edge, gives \(\sum_{p\le y}a_p^2\log p \sim y^2/2\). So this term is \(-x/2 + o(x)\), and higher powers are \(O(x^{2/3})\). Isolating the primes, \[ T_E(e^u) = \tfrac12 - r - \sum_{\gamma\ne 0}\frac{e^{i\gamma u}}{1+i\gamma} + o(1). \] The oscillating series is a Besicovitch almost-periodic function of mean zero. Hence \(\mathfrak M_E(U)\to\tfrac12 - r\). The \(\tfrac12\) is the symplectic offset. Its origin is the same as the \(\sqrt2\) in Goldfeld's theorem, and I generalise it in §6.

Derived(Crest variance law, under GRH and LI.) If the positive ordinates \(\gamma\) are simple and linearly independent over \(\Q\), Parseval for almost-periodic functions gives \(\lim_U \mathfrak V_E(U) = \sum_{\gamma\ne0}(1+\gamma^2)^{-1}\). The Hadamard product \(\Lambda(s) = e^{A+Bs}\prod_\rho(1-s/\rho)e^{s/\rho}\), with the functional equation forcing \(\operatorname{Re}B = -\sum_\rho\operatorname{Re}\rho^{-1}\), gives \(\operatorname{Re}\Lambda'/\Lambda(s) = \sum_\rho \operatorname{Re}(s-\rho)^{-1}\). At \(s=2\) each off-centre zero contributes \(1/(1+\gamma^2)\) and the central zero contributes \(r\). Therefore \[ \boxed{\ \lim_{U\to\infty}\mathfrak V_E(U) = \mathfrak B_E - r\ } \qquad\text{and}\qquad \boxed{\ \mathfrak V_E - \mathfrak M_E = \tfrac12\log N - \log 2\pi + \tfrac12 - \gamma_{\mathrm E} + \tfrac{L'}{L}(E,2).\ } \] The second identity combines the two estimators so that the unknown rank cancels. Its right-hand side contains no information about zeros at all.

Theorem(Budget inequality, unconditional given modularity.) Every zero has real part in \((\tfrac12,\tfrac32)\), so \(\operatorname{Re}(2-\rho)^{-1}>0\) for every \(\rho\). Hence \(r \le \mathfrak B_E\). This is the explicit-formula rank bound in Mestre's tradition. In the present language: the centre cannot spend more than the budget, and \(\mathfrak V_E = \mathfrak B_E - r\) is the slack carried by the off-centre zeros.

Theorem(Goldfeld 1982, sharpened by Conrad 2005.) If \(\prod_{p\le x}L_p(E,1)^{-1}\sim C_E(\log x)^{r'}\) for some \(C_E\neq 0\) and \(r'\), then \(L(E,s)\) satisfies GRH, \(r'=r\), and \(C_E = \sqrt2\,e^{r\gamma_{\mathrm E}}\, r!/L^{(r)}(E,1)\). The \(\sqrt2\) is the exponential of the symplectic offset \(\tfrac12\log 2\) that arises from the prime squares.

The crest mean recovers \(\tfrac12 - r\) for every rank, to within \(0.013\), \(0.032\), \(0.071\), \(0.057\) and \(0.144\). The log-log slope recovers \(r\). The variance law agrees to four digits for 11a1 (\(0.2532\) against \(0.2531\)) and to between 5 and 16 percent for the others. Between \(10^{6}\) and \(10^{7}\) it moved toward the prediction in every case: for 5077a1 it went from 0.970 to 1.116 against a target of 1.331, and for 37a1 from 0.358 to 0.345 against 0.374. The partial-product constant agrees with Goldfeld's formula, \(\sqrt2\) included, to between 2 and 9 percent. Without the \(\sqrt2\), the measured constants would miss by about 41 percent.

Measured(Spectral readout.) I took the Hann-tapered Fourier transform of \(T_E(e^u) - \mathfrak M_E\) in \(u\). For 11a1 its peaks fall at \(6.36, 8.59, 10.04, 11.49\), against the first four ordinates \(6.363, 8.604, 10.036, 11.451\) from PARI's lfunzeros. So the zeros of \(L(E,s)\) are read off the point counts to within \(0.04\). For the higher-rank curves the window resolution \(2\pi/U\approx 0.7\) blurs adjacent zeros, but the lowest ordinate is still caught: \(2.87\) against \(2.876\) for 389a1, and \(2.07\) against \(2.052\) for 5077a1. A stronger test is reconstruction. I synthesised \(\tfrac12 - r - 2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{0<\gamma<40}e^{i\gamma u}/(1+i\gamma)\) from the computed zeros and correlated it with the measured \(T_E\). The correlations are \(0.849, 0.886, 0.943, 0.960, 0.976\) for ranks 0 to 4, with residual RMS about \(0.3\). That residual is accounted for by the truncation at \(\gamma<40\), whose tail has mean square \(\mathfrak B - r - \sum_{|\gamma|<40}(1+\gamma^2)^{-1}\approx 0.07\) to \(0.14\), together with the \(o(1)\) terms.

6. The graded symmetry-offset law

DerivedThe construction of §4 works for any self-dual motive \(M\) of weight \(w\) with an automorphic \(L\)-function. Write \(c = (w+1)/2\) for its centre, \(\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}\) for its Frobenius–Schur indicator (\(+1\) orthogonal, \(-1\) symplectic), \(r\) for its central order, and \(\lambda_M(p)\) for its Frobenius trace. Define \(T_M(x) = x^{-c}\sum_{p\le x}\lambda_M(p)\log p\). The prime squares contribute \(\sum_{p\le\sqrt x}\lambda_M(p^2)\log p \approx \varepsilon\,x^{c}/(2c)\), because the unitary average of \(\operatorname{tr}\Frob^2\) is \(\varepsilon\). Each central zero contributes \(-x^{c}/c\). Each off-centre zero \(c+i\gamma\) contributes \(-x^{c+i\gamma}/(c+i\gamma)\). Hence \[ \mathfrak M_M = -\frac{\varepsilon + 2r}{2c},\qquad \mathfrak V_M = \sum_{\gamma\neq0}\frac{1}{c^2+\gamma^2} = \frac{\mathfrak B_M}{c} - \frac{r}{c^2},\qquad \mathfrak B_M = \operatorname{Re}\frac{\Lambda'}{\Lambda}(M,2c). \] The budget inequality generalises to \(r\le c\,\mathfrak B_M\), unconditionally. For \(M = h^1(E)\), with \(w=1\), \(c=1\) and \(\varepsilon=-1\), this is §4.

The sign of the offset flips with the indicator, as predicted. Orthogonal \(\mathrm{Sym}^2\) has its mean pulled below zero, and symplectic \(\mathrm{Sym}^1\) and \(\mathrm{Sym}^3\) have theirs pushed above. The variance law holds to within 1 percent for \(\mathrm{Sym}^2\). For \(\mathrm{Sym}^3\) the agreement is looser (8 and 13 percent), because higher weight makes the \(O(x^{-1/2+\epsilon})\) corrections in the prime-square term relatively larger at this \(x\). The central zero of \(L(\mathrm{Sym}^3 37a1,s)\) is caught by the mean: \(-0.185\) is much nearer \(-\tfrac14\) than the \(+\tfrac14\) predicted for \(r=0\).

7. The height crest: Mordell–Weil lattices and Manin growth

The crest exponents also come back as exponents of global counting, along two routes.

Theorem(Néron; the lattice route.) Let \(E(\Q)/E_{\mathrm{tors}} \cong \Z^{r}\) carry the Néron–Tate pairing, with Gram matrix \(G\) on a basis and regulator \(\Reg_E = \det G\). Then \(\#\{P\in E(\Q):\hat h(P)\le t\} \sim |E_{\mathrm{tors}}|\,V_r\,t^{r/2}/\sqrt{\Reg_E}\), where \(V_r = \pi^{r/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac r2+1)\) is the volume of the unit \(r\)-ball. This is the Gauss circle problem in the Mordell–Weil lattice. Since the naive and canonical heights differ by a bounded amount, points of naive height at most \(B\) number \(\asymp(\log B)^{r/2}\). So the central crest \(r\) becomes the height exponent \(r/2\) on the logarithmic scale.

MeasuredI found generators with ellrank and saturated them at all primes up to 100 with ellsaturation. This recovers regulators \(0.051111\), \(0.152460\), \(0.417144\) and \(1.504345\) for ranks 1 to 4, matching the tabulated values, and the analytic order of Ш comes out \(1.000000\) in each case. I counted lattice points with \(n^{\mathsf T}Gn\le t\) for \(t\) up to 160. The ratio of count to ball prediction at \(t=160\) is \(0.992\), \(0.9997\), \(0.9975\) and \(1.0001\). The rank-4 lattice holds \(103005\) points against a prediction of \(102995\).

Theorem(Manin's conjecture, proved for toric varieties and products of projective spaces.) For Fano \(X\) with anticanonical height \(H\), the number of rational points of height at most \(B\) is asymptotic to \(c_X B(\log B)^{\rho-1}\). On the polynomial scale, then, the order-one crest \(\rho = \kk^{(1)}\) becomes the log-exponent \(\rho-1\).

MeasuredOn \(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\) with the \(\mathcal O(1,1)\) height \(H(x)H(y)\), I counted exactly using \(\#\{P \in \mathbb P^1(\Q): H(P)=h\} = 4\varphi(h)\) for every \(h\ge1\), where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient. This is corrected in §14; the first edition used \(2\varphi(h)\), and derived its prediction from the same wrong count. At \(B = 10^{3},\dots,10^{6}\), the ratio \(N(B)/B^2\log B\) takes the values \(3.727, 3.533, 3.417, 3.341\). Fitting \(c + c'/\log B\) gives \(c = 2.9535\), against the predicted \(288/\pi^4 = 2.9566\), with \(c' = 5.342\). The power of \(\log B\) is \(1 = \rho - 1\). On \(\mathbb P^2\), primitive triples with \(\max|x_i|\le T\) number \(3.3318\,T^3\) at \(T=1000\), against \(4/\zeta(3) = 3.3276\), with log-exponent \(0 = \rho - 1\).

The crest–height dictionaryOne root datum, read at two depths, predicts two growth laws. The order-one crest \(\kk^{(1)} = \rho\) governs Euler-product growth \((\log x)^{\rho}\) and, for Fano \(X\), polynomial-scale height growth \(B(\log B)^{\rho-1}\). The central crest \(r\), read through \(\mathfrak M = \tfrac12-r\), governs partial-product growth \((\log x)^{r}\) and logarithmic-scale height growth \((\log B)^{r/2}\). The Mordell–Weil lattice is where the two scales meet: its covolume \(\sqrt{\Reg}\) is the denominator of the height law, and as §8 shows, it is also the denominator of the crest constant.

8. BSD in crest form

DerivedCombine Goldfeld's constant with the BSD leading-term formula \(L^{(r)}(E,1)/r! = \Omega_E\,\Reg_E\,|\Sha|\prod_p c_p\,/\,|E_{\mathrm{tors}}|^{2}\), where \(\Omega_E\) is the real period and the \(c_p\) are the Tamagawa numbers. The \(L\)-value cancels and the factorial disappears: \[ \boxed{\ C_E\cdot \Reg_E\cdot|\Sha(E)| = \frac{\sqrt2\,e^{r\gamma_{\mathrm E}}\,|E_{\mathrm{tors}}|^{2}}{\Omega_E\prod_p c_p}\ } \] The left side contains no \(L\)-function. It is the asymptotic constant of a product of local point counts, times the squared covolume of the Mordell–Weil lattice, times the order of Ш. The right side is archimedean and Tamagawa data. Read this way, BSD says that local point counts, through their crest constant, and the global lattice, through its covolume, are dual with a fixed archimedean exchange rate.

MeasuredWith \(C_E\) taken from the partial product at \(x=10^{7}\), and \(\Reg_E\) and \(\Omega_E\prod c_p/|E_{\mathrm{tors}}|^2\) from PARI's ellbsd, the ratios of left to right side are \(0.978\), \(0.960\), \(1.028\), \(1.092\) and \(1.019\) for ranks 0 to 4. Each discrepancy is within the drift of \(C_E\) over the last decade of \(x\), which Table 2 shows to be several percent.

9. New conjectures

RetractionThe \((\log N)^2\) scaling originally stated in Conjecture A is withdrawn. The 492-curve twist test in §12 refutes it. The derived bound \(\mathfrak D_E/U\) stands. The scaling law is replaced by Conjecture A′, which says the driver is the normalized lowest zero, not a power of \(\log N\). The original text is kept below for the record.

Conjecture A (withdrawn)(Crest uncertainty principle.) Let \(\mathfrak D_E = 2\sum_{\gamma>0}\big(\gamma\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}\big)^{-1}\). Integrating the almost-periodic series term by term gives, under GRH, \(|\mathfrak M_E(U)-(\tfrac12-r)|\le \mathfrak D_E/U + o(1)\), and this part I regard as derived. For our five curves the bound \(\mathfrak D_E/U\) is \(0.026, 0.039, 0.085, 0.149, 0.254\), against observed errors of \(0.013, 0.032, 0.071, 0.057, 0.144\), so it holds in every case. The conjecture is about the size of \(\mathfrak D_E\). I conjecture that over all \(E/\Q\) ordered by conductor, \(\mathfrak D_E \asymp (\log N)^2\) for a positive proportion of curves, and \(\mathfrak D_E\gg(\log N)^{2}\) whenever \(r\ge2\). The heuristic: Katz–Sarnak statistics put the lowest ordinate \(\gamma_1\) at scale \(1/\log N\), and \(\mathfrak D_E\ge 2/\big(\gamma_1\sqrt{1+\gamma_1^2}\big)\). The consequence is a complexity law. Certifying rank from point counts alone needs \(\log x \gg (\log N)^2\), so \(x\) must be super-polynomial in \(N\). This would be a structural obstruction to any purely local rank algorithm based on the central crest. It would be refuted by a family with \(\gamma_1\log N\to\infty\), or by a local method that certifies rank with \(\log x = o((\log N)^2)\). The measured trend \(\mathfrak D_E = 0.24, 0.36, 0.77, 1.36, 2.32\) against \(\log N = 2.40, 3.61, 5.96, 8.53, 12.36\) is consistent with roughly linear growth at these small conductors, so the data neither confirm nor refute the conjectured quadratic growth yet.

Conjecture B(Graded crest law, unconditional form.) For every self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation \(\pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb A_\Q)\) with central order \(r\), indicator \(\varepsilon\) and centre \(c\), I conjecture that \(\mathfrak M_\pi(U)\to -(\varepsilon+2r)/2c\) holds without assuming LI. I further conjecture that the weaker variance statement \(\limsup_U \mathfrak V_\pi(U)\le \mathfrak B_\pi/c - r/c^2\) is equivalent to GRH for \(L(\pi,s)\). The forward direction follows from Parseval with Bessel's inequality in place of LI. The reverse direction is the content: a zero off the line, at \(\beta+i\gamma\) with \(\beta>c\), adds a term of size \(x^{\beta-c}\) that makes \(\mathfrak V_\pi(U)\) grow like \(e^{2(\beta-c)U}\). This does not follow from the zero existing. It requires excluding cancellation among off-line zeros, which is the standard Landau-type difficulty. If B holds, then a sequence of rigorous interval-arithmetic computations of \(\mathfrak V_\pi(U)\), each staying below the budget, would give an increasingly stringent form of evidence for GRH, tested against a target fixed in advance. That is not a proof.

Conjecture C(Crest–height exponent law for the intermediate regime.) For a smooth projective \(X/\Q\) whose rational points are Zariski dense, and whose middle cohomology contains a self-dual motive \(M_{\mathrm{mid}}\) of odd weight with central order \(r_{\mathrm{mid}}\), I conjecture that the counting function of rational points on a suitable open subset, with respect to an ample height, has the form \(B^{a}(\log B)^{b}\). Here \(a\) is determined by the order-one crest through the effective cone, as in Batyrev–Manin, and \(b\) is an affine function of \(\kk^{(1)}\) and \(r_{\mathrm{mid}}\) together. The Fano case \(b=\rho-1\) and the abelian-variety case \(b = r/2\) on the log scale are the two endpoints. The cubic threefold is the first test case. Its intermediate Jacobian is \(5\)-isotypic for the \(j=0\) curve, as §3 read off from \(N_p\), so it is the natural place to look for a central-crest contribution to Manin-type counts. This is the most speculative of the four conjectures, and I have no numerical evidence for it yet.

Conjecture D(BSD crest form as a computable certificate.) The identity in §8 holds for every \(E/\Q\). Moreover, the left side, computed from a partial product to \(x\) and a saturated lattice, converges at the rate \(1+O(\mathfrak D_E/\log x)\) uniformly in \(E\). If true, then \(|\Sha(E)|\) can be estimated from point counts and a lattice basis without evaluating any \(L\)-function. Rounding to a perfect square would turn the estimate into a candidate for the exact order of Ш. Its five-curve test is in §8.

10. What the calculus adds, and where it stops

The capacity gain is operational. Three conjectures that are normally stated in incompatible languages become one family of estimators on the single integer sequence \(N_p\). The Tate conjecture appears as \(\kk^{(j)} = \) rank of algebraic cycles. GRH and BSD appear as \(\mathfrak M = \tfrac12-r\), \(\mathfrak V = \mathfrak B - r\), and the crest form of BSD. Manin and Néron appear as the height exponents \(\rho-1\) and \(r/2\). Each estimator has a closed-form target computable before any data are gathered, and a finite-window error bound, so each one is a falsification instrument rather than a heuristic plot. The orbit-compressed counter makes the order-one side exact and cheap in every dimension. The balanced expansion extracts degree-by-degree Frobenius traces from one integer. Second moments of normalized traces read isotypic multiplicities. The variance–mean combination \(\mathfrak V-\mathfrak M\) gives a rank-free consistency check on any claimed rank computation. The limits are just as definite. Each derived identity rests on GRH, and the variance identity also needs LI. Conjecture A, if true, says the central crest cannot certify rank efficiently at large conductor. And no part of this program replaces a proof. The natural next steps are three. First, interval-certified evaluation of \(\mathfrak V_E(U)\) against \(\mathfrak B_E\), which tests Conjecture B in its rigorous form. Second, a twist family of conductors up to \(10^{8}\), which tests the \((\log N)^2\) scaling of Conjecture A. Third, rational-point counts on the Fermat cubic threefold, which tests Conjecture C.

Part II. Certification and the uncertainty law

11. Interval-certified crest statistics to \(x = 10^{8}\)

The window statistics of §4 can be computed with no quadrature and no rounding error. That is the step from measured to certified. On a prime gap \(p_k\le x

The budget \(\mathfrak B_E\) is certified the same way. For good \(p\), the term is \(\tfrac{L_p'}{L_p}(2) = -\log p\,(a_pp^{-2}-2p^{-3})/(1-a_pp^{-2}+p^{-3})\), summed exactly in Arb to \(X\). For bad \(p\) it is the corresponding single-factor expression. The tail uses Deligne's bound and the Rosser–Schoenfeld inequality \(\theta(t)<1.01624\,t\). Partial summation gives \(\sum_{p>X}|\tfrac{L_p'}{L_p}(2)|\le(1+2X^{-3/2})\big(6.0974\,X^{-1/2}-2\theta(X)X^{-3/2}\big)\), which is \(4.1\cdot10^{-4}\) at \(X=10^8\). The certified budgets agree with PARI's floating-point values to every displayed digit.

MeasuredThe certified variance follows the finite-window zero synthesis, not the limit. At \(10^8\) the relative discrepancies against the synthesis are \(1.2\%\), \(1.9\%\), \(0.15\%\), \(2.6\%\) and \(2.4\%\). The discrepancies against \(\mathfrak B-r\) reach \(16\%\). The difference \(\mathfrak V(U)-(\mathfrak B-r)\) is therefore almost entirely the cross-term \(\sum_{\gamma\ne\gamma'}c_\gamma\bar c_{\gamma'}\,U^{-1}\!\int e^{i(\gamma-\gamma')u}du\), which LI sends to zero only as \(U\to\infty\). At \(U\approx11\), close pairs of ordinates (\(4.471, 4.754\) for 5077a1) are still far from averaged out. This forces a correction to Conjecture B. A finite-window certified \(\mathfrak V(U)\) can exceed the limit \(\mathfrak B-r\), and does so here for 11a1 and 389a1. So the rigorous test is not "\(\mathfrak V(U)\) stays below budget". It is \(\mathfrak V(U)\le\mathfrak B-r+K_E/U\), with \(K_E=\sum_{\gamma\ne\gamma'}2|c_\gamma c_{\gamma'}|/|\gamma-\gamma'|\) computed from the zeros. A \(\mathfrak V(U)\) growing faster than every such envelope would certify a zero off the line, given the non-cancellation hypothesis of Conjecture B.

MeasuredThe certified mean sits below the zero synthesis by \(-0.007, -0.026, -0.041, -0.048, -0.084\) at \(10^8\) for ranks 0 to 4. This offset is correlated with rank and shrinks by 20–30% per decade of \(x\). Its source is the step \(\sum_{p\le\sqrt x}(a_p^2-2p)\log p\approx -x/2\). Curves of high rank have large \(|a_p|\) at small primes, so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{Sym}^2}(p)=a_p^2-p\) is biased upward early, giving a transient of order \(x^{-1/4}\) that a synthesis from the zeros of \(L(E,s)\) alone cannot see. Including the prime squares exactly, at \(X=10^7\), moves the residuals from \([-0.009,-0.109]\), ordered by rank, to \([-0.010,-0.038]\), with no rank ordering. What remains is consistent with truncating the zeros at \(\gamma\le100\) and with the prime cubes.

12. The uncertainty law, measured on 492 twists

The quantity \(\mathfrak D_E=\sum_{\gamma\ne0}\big(|\gamma|\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}\big)^{-1}\) of Conjecture A can be bracketed rigorously, given a complete list of zeros below \(T_0\). Every tail term satisfies \(1\le\sqrt{1+\gamma^{-2}}\le\sqrt{1+T_0^{-2}}\) times \((1+\gamma^2)^{-1}\), and the tail of \(\sum(1+\gamma^2)^{-1}\) is exactly \(R=\mathfrak B-r-\sum_{0<|\gamma|\le T_0}(1+\gamma^2)^{-1}\) by the Hadamard identity. So \(\mathfrak D_E\in[\mathfrak D_{\le T_0}+R,\ \mathfrak D_{\le T_0}+\sqrt{1+T_0^{-2}}\,R]\). With \(T_0=4\), the bracket width never exceeded \(0.05\). I computed this for the quadratic twists of 11a1 by every fundamental discriminant with \(|d|\le400\), plus 250 sampled in \((400,3000]\). That is 492 curves with conductor \(N\) from about \(10^2\) to \(9.9\cdot10^{7}\): 204 of rank 0, 262 of rank 1, and 26 of rank 2.

MeasuredA fit to \(\mathfrak D\sim(\log N)^\alpha\) gives apparent exponents \(2.22\) at rank 0 and \(2.17\) at rank 1. But the binned medians of \(\mathfrak D/(\log N\log\log N)\) keep drifting, and at rank 0 the residual scatter is enormous (RSS \(\approx15\,000\)). The scatter has a definite cause. Set \(L'=\log(\sqrt N/2\pi)\), so that the ordinate density near height 0 is \(L'/\pi\). Let \(\delta_1=\gamma_1L'/\pi\) be the normalized lowest zero. The heuristic sum \(\mathfrak D\approx\tfrac{2L'}\pi\sum_k(k+\delta_1)^{-1}\) over low-lying zeros predicts \(\mathfrak D/L'\approx\tfrac2\pi\delta_1^{-1}+\beta\log L'+c\). The least-squares fits are below.

At rank 0 the coefficient of \(\delta_1^{-1}\) is \(0.631\) against \(2/\pi=0.6366\), and the model explains \(99.56\%\) of the variance. The lowest-zero statistics agree with Katz–Sarnak symmetry types, which is classical and not my claim. Rank-0 twists have even sign, and the \(\mathrm{SO}(\text{even})\) joint density has no factor that vanishes as an angle approaches 0, so \(\delta_1\) has positive density near 0. The observed minimum is \(0.065\), for \(d=-2531\) at \(N\approx7.0\cdot10^7\), where \(\mathfrak D=77.3\). Rank-1 twists are \(\mathrm{SO}(\text{odd})\), whose forced central zero repels the first ordinate quadratically, giving minimum \(0.298\). The rank-2 stratum is pushed further still, with minimum \(1.133\). The log coefficient \(b\) comes out between \(0.41\) and \(0.55\), below the naive \(2/\pi\). Downgraded in §15The coefficient \(a\approx2/\pi\) in Table 5 is largely forced by the definition of \(\mathfrak D_E\), so it is not evidence for a law. What survives of Conjecture A′ is stated in §15.

Conjecture A′ (superseded)(Crest uncertainty law, revised.) For \(E/\Q\) of conductor \(N\), set \(L'_E=\log(\sqrt N/2\pi)\) and let \(\delta_1(E)\) be the normalized lowest positive ordinate. Then \[ \mathfrak D_E=\frac{2}{\pi}\,L'_E\Big(\frac1{\delta_1(E)}+\beta_{r}\log L'_E+O(1)\Big), \] where \(\beta_r\) depends only on the symmetry type. The measured values are \(\beta_0\approx0.86\), \(\beta_1\approx0.74\) and \(\beta_2\approx0.64\) in units of \(2/\pi\). The consequence for computation is this. Read through the bound \(\mathfrak D_E/U\), certifying the rank from the central crest requires \[ \log x\ \gtrsim\ \frac{\log N}{\pi}\Big(\frac1{\delta_1}+\beta_r\log\log N\Big), \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad x\ \gtrsim\ N^{(1/\pi)\,(\delta_1^{-1}+\beta_r\log\log N)}. \] The cost is super-polynomial in \(N\) only through \(\log\log N\) for typical curves. It blows up as \(N^{1/(\pi\delta_1)}\) on exactly the hard cases: rank-0 curves with a near-central zero, which are the ones where rank 0 and rank 2 are numerically confusable. For \(d=-2531\), the exponent is about \(5\), so \(x\approx10^{39}\). Because \(\delta_1\) has positive density at 0 in the even family, the family average of \(\mathfrak D_E\) diverges logarithmically with the height cut-off, while the median stays at order \(L'\log L'\). This replaces the withdrawn \((\log N)^2\) form. It would be refuted by an even-sign family in which \(\mathfrak D_E/L'\) is uncorrelated with \(\delta_1^{-1}\), or by a rank certificate from local data alone using \(\log x=o(\mathfrak D_E)\).

13. Status after Part II

Conjecture A in its \((\log N)^2\) form is refuted. Conjecture A′ replaces it, with \(R^2=0.9956\) at rank 0 and the predicted coefficient \(2/\pi\) recovered to \(1\%\). The \(\beta_r\) shortfall is open. Conjecture B is sharpened. Its finite-window content is now an envelope test, \(\mathfrak V(U)\le\mathfrak B-r+K_E/U\), not a bare budget test, because certified finite-window variances exceed the limit on two of five curves. The ingredients that are now rigorous, rather than measured, are the certified \(\mathfrak V(U)\), the certified \(\mathfrak M(U)\) and the certified \(\mathfrak B_E\). The comparison between them is still conditional on GRH and LI, through the zero synthesis. The rank-correlated mean offset is identified as a \(\mathrm{Sym}^2\) transient, and including the prime squares exactly removes it. Conjectures C and D are unchanged. The next decisive computation is to certify \(K_E\) from interval-certified zeros, for example with Arb's Dirichlet and modular-form machinery or with Booker's rigorous \(L\)-function methods. That would make the envelope test of Conjecture B fully unconditional on the numerical side.

Part III. Audit, errata and what survives

14. Errata

Erratum 1(Manin constant on \(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\).) The first edition counted \(2\varphi(h)\) points of \(\mathbb P^1(\Q)\) of exact height \(h\ge2\). The correct count is \(4\varphi(h)\): for each \(h\) there are \(8\varphi(h)\) primitive pairs \((a,b)\) with \(\max(|a|,|b|)=h\), identified in pairs by sign. I verified this by brute force for \(h\le7\). The first edition's predicted constant \(72/\pi^4\) was derived from the same wrong count, so its agreement with the data was circular: it checked the asymptotic algebra, not the arithmetic. With the correct count, the asymptotic constant is \(2\cdot(12/\pi^2)^2=288/\pi^4=2.9566\), and the fit gives \(2.9535\). The log exponent \(1=\rho-1\) and the crest–height dictionary are unaffected. The \(\mathbb P^2\) count was correct.

Erratum 2(Exactness of the counter.) The class algebra first computed its cyclotomic numbers with a rounded float64 FFT. Every count involved is at most \(p<1500\), so the rounding margin was enormous, but that is not a proof. The counter now uses exact int64 direct convolution, which is provably exact since every intermediate value is below \(p^2<2^{63}\). It reproduces every crest value in Table 1 and §3 identically.

Erratum 3(Completeness of zero lists.) PARI's documentation warns that lfunzeros can miss zeros, so every statement that uses a complete zero list below \(T_0\) is conditional on that completeness, not certified. Two facts limit the damage. First, the lower bracket \(\mathfrak D_E\ge\mathfrak D_{\le T_0}^{\text{found}}+R\) is robust to missed zeros. A missed zero \(\gamma\) moves \(1/(1+\gamma^2)\) into \(R\), and its true contribution \(1/(|\gamma|\sqrt{1+\gamma^2})\) is at least that much, so the lower bound remains valid given GRH and the certified \(\mathfrak B\). Only the upper bracket depends on completeness. Second, as an empirical check, recomputing all 492 zero lists with 4× finer subdivision (divz=32) changed no zero count. A rigorous completeness certificate needs Turing's method or Booker's validated \(L\)-function computations, and I have not done that. The finite-window zero synthesis in Table 4 has the same status.

15. The uncertainty constant after removing the definitional term

By definition, \(\mathfrak D_E\) contains the pair \(\pm\gamma_1\), which contributes exactly \(2/(\gamma_1\sqrt{1+\gamma_1^2})\). Writing \(\delta_1=\gamma_1L'/\pi\), this is \((2/\pi)L'\,\delta_1^{-1}(1+\gamma_1^2)^{-1/2}\). So a regression of \(\mathfrak D/L'\) on \(\delta_1^{-1}\) recovers about \(2/\pi\) for any zero configuration in which \(\gamma_1\) is small and dominant. The fit in Table 5 was mostly the definition talking. I confirmed this on the same data. At rank 0 (201 twists with \(N>200\)), the definitional term plus a constant alone explains \(R^2=0.9889\), with slope \(0.997\).

Two things follow, and they are less exciting than the first edition claimed. First, the second zero enters the same way as the first: adding \(\delta_2^{-1}\) raises the residual \(R^2\) to about \(0.92\), and its coefficient \(e\approx0.8\) is again close to the \(2/\pi\) scale, so this too is definitional. \(\mathfrak D_E\) is simply a linear statistic of the low-lying zeros, and peeling off zeros one at a time will keep "explaining" it. Second, what is not definitional is how \(\mathfrak R_E\) grows with \(L'\). After removing the first two zeros, the coefficient of \(\log L'\) is \(0.30\) to \(0.36\), about half the naive uniform-density value \(2/\pi\). The strong negative correlation between \(\delta_1\) and the gap \(\delta_2-\delta_1\) shows that the low zeros are not independent. When the first zero is low, the second sits further from it.

Conjecture A″(What survives.) I withdraw any claim of a new law for \(\mathfrak D_E\). The surviving statement has two parts. The first is a complexity consequence, which stands: certifying rank from the central crest alone requires \(\log x\gtrsim\mathfrak D_E\), and \(\mathfrak D_E\) is dominated by the reciprocal of the lowest normalized zero, so the hard cases are exactly the curves with near-central zeros. The second is a statistical question. For quadratic twists at finite conductor, the family distribution of \(\mathfrak D_E\), and in particular the sub-\(2/\pi\) growth rate of the residual \(\mathfrak R_E\), should be predicted by the finite-conductor random-matrix models for low-lying zeros of elliptic curve families. The specific candidate is the excised orthogonal ensemble of Dueñez, Huynh, Keating, Miller and Snaith, which models the repulsion of the first zero from the centre caused by the discreteness of central \(L\)-values, not by the conductor-independent Katz–Sarnak limit. This is falsifiable: simulate the excised ensemble at matching effective matrix size \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx L'\), compute the same linear statistic, and compare the distribution and the \(\log L'\) slope with Table 6. I have not run that simulation. Until it is run, A″ is a well-posed question, not evidence.

16. On enlarging the root datum

One proposal from the audit is to enlarge the root datum to \(\mathcal R(X)=(\{N_{p^m}\},\{\mathfrak o_{p,k}\},\{J^k_p\})\), adding extension-field counts, local lifting obstructions and jet data. Most of this adds nothing where the calculus already works. At a prime of good reduction, the counts \(N_{p^m}\) for all \(m\) are determined by the characteristic polynomials of Frobenius, and for curves of genus 1 by \(N_p\) alone. Hensel's lemma gives \(\#X(\Z/p^k)=N_p\,p^{d(k-1)}\) for smooth models, so lifting obstructions vanish and jet counts carry no information beyond \(N_p\). The enlarged datum becomes informative at bad primes and on singular models. There the \(p\)-adic counts \(\#X(\Z/p^k)\) are governed by Igusa's local zeta function, whose poles encode resolution data, as in Denef's work. That is a genuine extension of the calculus: a "bad-prime crest" reading discrepancies and log-canonical thresholds the way \(\kk^{(j)}\) reads Tate classes. It is not a way to strengthen the good-prime results reported here.

Part IV. The residual is arithmetic, not universal

17. The excised orthogonal ensemble, tested out of sample

Current-edition correction. Historical finding: the initial excised-ensemble result and normalization were later corrected. See §§35, 41–48 and the current edition ledger; do not treat the original out-of-sample p-values as final.

Erratum (§38)The tests in this section mapped data to eigenangles by \(\theta=\gamma N/L'\). The correct unfolding is \(\theta=\gamma L'/N\), as the parallel session pointed out. The numbers below are superseded by §38. The rejection of the low-lying residual survives the correction. The second-gap rejection does not.

Conjecture A″ asked whether the finite-conductor excised orthogonal ensemble (EOE) of Dueñez, Huynh, Keating, Miller and Snaith reproduces the non-definitional residual of \(\mathfrak D_E\). I simulated Haar \(\mathrm{SO}(2N)\) for \(N=3,\dots,10\), with 150 000 to 200 000 matrices per size. Following the discretization of central values \(L(E_d,1)\propto c_d^{2}/\sqrt{|d|}\) (Waldspurger, Kohnen–Zagier), I excised matrices with \(\Lambda_A(1)=\prod_j(2-2\cos\theta_j)<C\,e^{-N/2}\). The 195 rank-0 twists with \(\operatorname{round}(\lambda L')\ge3\) were assigned to matrix size \(N=\operatorname{round}(\lambda L')\), with angles \(\theta=\gamma N/L'\). Four statistics were compared: \(\delta_1\), the gaps \(\delta_2-\delta_1\) and \(\delta_3-\delta_2\), and the low-lying residual \(R_1=\sum_{k\ge2,\ \theta_k\le1}2/(\theta_k\sqrt{1+\theta_k^2})/N\). Both parameters were fitted on \(\delta_1\) and the first gap only. The other two statistics and the \(\delta_1\)–gap correlation were held out, and their p-values come from a parametric bootstrap with 300 replicates.

MeasuredExcision is real. It cuts the \(\delta_1\) discrepancy from \(0.224\) to \(0.064\), which confirms that the first zero of the rank-0 twists is repelled from the centre more strongly than the conductor-independent Katz–Sarnak limit allows. But the EOE does not reproduce the configuration beyond the first zero. Even with both parameters fitted, the second gap, the residual and the correlation are rejected at levels of 0.3% to 4%. Two caveats apply: matrix sizes are integers between 3 and 8, so the size binning is coarse, and four statistics were tested. Neither caveat accounts for a rejection at p = 0.003. The statistical half of Conjecture A″ is refuted in this form: no universal matrix model with these two parameters reproduces the residual.

18. The residual is set by the smallest primes

MeasuredTwisting by \(d\) multiplies \(a_p\) by \(\chi_d(p)\), so the twists form arithmetic subfamilies according to \(\chi_d(p)\) at small \(p\). Splitting the 200 rank-0 twists by \(\chi_d(2)\in\{-1,0,1\}\) gives low-lying residual means of \(0.150\), \(0.245\) and \(0.305\), and first-gap means of \(1.382\), \(1.087\) and \(0.989\). Permutation p-values are at their floor, \(2\cdot10^{-4}\), which survives Bonferroni correction over the 15 tests run. The distribution of \(\delta_1\) itself does not depend on \(\chi_d(2)\) (p = 0.59). The same direction appears at \(p=3\) and \(p=5\), with weaker but significant effects on the conductor-detrended full residual (p = 0.001 each). Across all three primes the rule is a single one: the residual decreases as the twisted coefficient \(a_p^{(d)}=\chi_d(p)a_p(11a1)\) increases. Negative small-prime coefficients pull the second and later zeros toward the centre, and positive ones push them out.

That is what Weil's explicit formula predicts. \(\mathfrak D_E\) is not an admissible explicit-formula sum, because its test function \(1/(|\gamma|\sqrt{1+\gamma^2})\) is singular at 0. But its smooth part is, and the prime side of the explicit formula weights \(a_p^{(d)}/\sqrt p\) by \(\log p/\sqrt p\) times a transform that decays in \(\log p/L'\). Using the predictor \(x_d=\sum_{p\le P}a_p^{(d)}(\log p/p)\max(0,1-\log p/2L')\), and regressing the residual on \(\log L'\) and \(x_d\), gives the following.

Three primes, 2, 3 and 5, explain about two-thirds of the conductor-detrended variance of the full residual at both rank 0 and rank 1. The coefficient is negative throughout, as the explicit formula requires. Extending to \(P=50\) dilutes the signal. That means my taper \(1-\log p/2L'\) decays far too slowly for this test function. It is not evidence against arithmetic control; a correctly derived weight is the natural refinement. With the predictor included, the rank-0 coefficient of \(\log L'\) moves from \(0.36\) to about \(0.42\). The sub-\(2/\pi\) slope is therefore partly a mixture effect across arithmetic subfamilies, whose share in the sample shifts with \(|d|\).

19. What this settles

The \(\mathfrak D_E\) line of investigation is now closed, with an honest result and no new law. \(\mathfrak D_E\) decomposes into three parts. The first is a definitional part, the reciprocal-zero terms of the lowest one or two ordinates, which explains about 99% of its variation. The second is an arithmetic part, set by the twisted coefficients at the smallest primes through the explicit formula, which explains about two-thirds of what remains. The third is a fluctuation part. Its universal component is consistent with excised orthogonal repulsion of the first zero, but beyond the first zero it is not reproduced by any excised ensemble I tested. The correct framework is a hybrid model in which an Euler product over small primes multiplies a random-matrix factor, in the spirit of Gonek, Hughes and Keating, with the excision built in. The complexity consequence is unchanged and now sharper. Certifying rank from the central crest costs \(\log x\gtrsim\mathfrak D_E\), which is dominated by the lowest zero. The arithmetic part means the cost is predictable in advance from \(\chi_d(2),\chi_d(3),\chi_d(5)\): twists with \(\chi_d(p)a_p<0\) at small primes have more low-lying zeros and so need longer prime ranges.

Conjecture E(Hybrid excised law.) For quadratic twists of a fixed \(E/\Q\) at fixed root number, the joint distribution of the first \(k\) normalized zeros, conditioned on the residue classes \((\chi_d(p))_{p\le P}\), converges as \(|d|\to\infty\) to an excised orthogonal ensemble whose cutoff and effective size are shifted by explicit functions of \(\sum_{p\le P}a_p^{(d)}\log p/\sqrt p\). Each conditional subfamily then passes the out-of-sample tests that the pooled family fails. This is falsifiable on the existing data once conditional samples are large enough. That needs about 2000 twists per \(\chi_d(2)\) class, roughly 10 times the present family, which is a few hours of computation.

Part V. A zero-free certified spectral calculator

20. The resolvent identity and its certified evaluation

DerivedThe parallel session derived the identity that makes this part possible, and I checked it independently. Put \(s=\sqrt t\). Then \(\Lambda(E,1+s)\,s^{-r}\) is an even entire function of order 1 whose zeros are \(s=\pm i\gamma\). So \(G(t)=\Lambda(E,1+\sqrt t)\,t^{-r/2}=\lambda_r\prod_{\gamma>0}(1+t/\gamma^2)\), and the resolvent is \(\mathscr H_E(t)=\tfrac{d}{dt}\log G(t)=\sum_{\gamma>0}(t+\gamma^2)^{-1}\). Combining this with \(\tfrac1\pi\int_0^1\frac{dt}{(t+\gamma^2)\sqrt{t(1-t)}}=\frac1{\gamma\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}}\) gives \[ \mathfrak D_E=\frac2\pi\int_0^1\frac{\mathscr H_E(t)}{\sqrt{t(1-t)}}\,dt. \] This converts a slowly convergent sum over zeros into a smooth integral of a function computable from \(\Lambda\) at real arguments. The parallel session evaluated it for 11a1 in mpmath, using numerical differentiation. I have made every step of that evaluation an Arb ball computation and extended it to all five curves.

The representation has three ingredients. Write \(c_n=2\pi n/\sqrt N\) and \(g_n(s)=\int_1^\infty e^{-c_ny}y^{s}\,dy=c_n^{-1-s}\Gamma(1+s,c_n)\). The Fricke involution gives \[ \Lambda(E,1+s)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\big[g_n(s)+w\,g_n(-s)\big],\qquad g_n(s)=c_n^{-1-s}\Gamma(1+s)-\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(-c_n)^j}{j!\,(1+j+s)}, \] and \(g_n'(s)=c_n^{-1-s}\Gamma(1+s)\big(\psi(1+s)-\log c_n\big)+\sum_j(-c_n)^j/\big(j!(1+j+s)^2\big)\). These are exact for \(|\operatorname{Re}s|<1\). The alternating series is evaluated in Arb at a working precision raised by \(c_n/\log2\) bits to absorb its cancellation. It is cut off once \(j>2c_n\), with tail bound \(2|T_J|\). The sum over \(n\) is cut at \(M\), with tail bound \((20\sqrt N/2\pi)\,e^{-c_{M+1}}/(1-e^{-2\pi/\sqrt N})\). That bound comes from \(|a_n|\le d(n)\sqrt n\le2n\) and \(\int_1^\infty e^{-cy}y^2dy\le5e^{-c}/c\). It covers values, \(s\)-derivatives and every Taylor coefficient. No numerical differentiation is used anywhere.

The quadrature bound needs no external input. Under GRH, \(\mathscr H_E\) is analytic for \(\operatorname{Re}t>-\gamma_1^2\). On the Bernstein ellipse with \(\operatorname{Re}t\ge-a\), where \(a=g^2/2\) for a certified lower bound \(g\le\gamma_1\), we have \(|\mathscr H_E|\le\frac{g^2+1}{g^2-a}\sum_{\gamma>0}(1+\gamma^2)^{-1}\). Since \(\mathscr H_E\) decreases on \(t>0\), \(\sum_{\gamma>0}(1+\gamma^2)^{-1}=\mathscr H_E(1)\le\mathscr H_E(t_1)\), where \(t_1\) is the largest node. Gauss–Chebyshev with \(m\) nodes is a \(2m\)-point trapezoid rule in \(\theta=\arccos x\), so its error in \(\mathfrak D\) is at most \(4M_H/(\rho^{2m}-1)\). The lower bound \(g\) comes from the moments in the next paragraph, so the whole certificate uses one sweep over the coefficients \(a_n\) and no zeros.

The moments come from the Taylor series at the centre. Set \(\lambda_k=[x^k]\,\Lambda(E,1+x)\), which is exactly 0 when \(1+w(-1)^k=0\). Then \(G(t)=\sum_i\lambda_{r+2i}t^i\), and \(\log(G/\lambda_r)=\sum_m(-1)^{m+1}p_mt^m/m\) yields the power sums \(p_m=\sum_{\gamma>0}\gamma^{-2m}\) as balls. Under GRH, \(p_m^{-1/2m}\le\gamma_1\le(p_m/p_{m+1})^{1/2}\) for every \(m\): the first inequality because \(p_m\ge\gamma_1^{-2m}\), the second because the ratio is a weighted mean of the \(\gamma^2\).

MeasuredFor 11a1 the certified ball contains the parallel session's mpmath value \(0.2541336435773785704647596071631157165\), and the two agree to all 35 digits. That is an independent confirmation of both the identity and their implementation. The certified \(\lambda_r\) agrees with \((\sqrt N/2\pi)\,L^{(r)}(E,1)/r!\) from PARI. Exactly what is rigorous needs stating carefully. \(\lambda_r\ne0\) is certified, so \(r_{\mathrm{an}}\le r\) as soon as the lower Taylor coefficients vanish. Those not forced to vanish by parity are hypotheses here. For 389a1 (\(L(E,1)=0\)) the vanishing is provable exactly through modular symbols. For 5077a1 (\(L'(E,1)=0\)) it follows from Gross–Zagier via Buhler–Gross–Zagier. For 234446a1 (\(L(E,1)=L''(E,1)=0\)) no proof is currently known. So the rank-4 certificate is conditional on its rank as well as on GRH, which interprets zeros as real ordinates and is used in the quadrature domain and the moment bounds. The ball computations themselves are unconditional.

22. Certified first zeros and certified complete zero lists

DerivedMoments and sign changes combine into a first-zero certificate that uses only two point evaluations. The function \(Z(\tau)\), taken as \(\operatorname{Re}\) or \(\operatorname{Im}\) of \(\sum_na_ng_n(i\tau)\) according to \(w\), is real on the critical line. A certified sign change on \([\tau_a,\tau_b]\) proves a zero of odd multiplicity there, unconditionally. If in addition \(p_m\tau_b^{2m}<2\) for some \(m\), then under GRH there is exactly one zero, counted with multiplicity, in \((0,\tau_b]\), because each such zero contributes at least \(\tau_b^{-2m}\) to \(p_m\). The zero is therefore the first zero, and it is simple. All five curves pass, with \(\tau_b-\tau_a=2\cdot10^{-12}\) and \(\min_mp_m\tau_b^{2m}\) between \(1.0000000002\) and \(1.0000238\).

Deflation extends this to whole lists, which answers the completeness objection of Erratum 3. Take every PARI seed zero up to a height \(T_{\max}\) and certify a sign change on \([\gamma_k-10^{-10},\gamma_k+10^{-10}]\) for each. Subtract the ball enclosures of \(\gamma_k^{-2m}\) for all certified zeros from \(p_m\). Under GRH the remainder \(R_m\ge0\) collects every other zero and every extra multiplicity. If \(R_m^{\text{upper}}<T^{-2m}\) for some \(m\), then the certified list is the complete list of zeros in \((0,T]\), and each is simple.

23. Status after Part V

The spectral side of the calculus now has a proof-producing core. From the exact coefficients \(a_n\), the conductor and the root number, one Arb sweep yields the following, conditional only on GRH and, for ranks 2 to 4, on the stated rank hypothesis: \(\lambda_r\); the power sums \(p_m\); two-sided enclosures of \(\gamma_1\); \(\mathfrak D_E\) to 31–36 digits; and, with seed zeros added, certified complete zero lists. The audit's Erratum 3 is resolved on these five curves at these heights. Two other results from the parallel session are confirmed independently. The \(\mathfrak D_{11a1}\) value agrees to 35 digits. The singular counting identity \(N_k(p;a,b)=p^{2k-\lceil k/a\rceil-\lceil k/b\rceil}+(p-1)\sum_{h=0}^{\lfloor(k-1)/ab\rfloor}p^{k-1+(ab-a-b)h}\) agreed with exhaustive enumeration in 175 of 175 cases, covering exponent pairs \((2,3),(3,2),(2,5),(3,4),(1,2),(3,5),(2,7)\), primes 2 to 7 and \(p^k\le40\,000\).

Three steps follow directly. First, the budget \(\mathfrak B_E=\operatorname{Re}\Lambda'/\Lambda(E,2)\) should be certified through this calculator, by moving the evaluation point slightly inside \(|\operatorname{Re}s|<1\) and using the monotonicity of \(\mathscr H_E\). That would replace the \(\pm4\cdot10^{-4}\) Euler-product budget and tighten every comparison in Parts II and IV by many orders of magnitude. Second, the twist family should be rerun with certified complete zero lists. That makes the Conjecture E test rigorous in its inputs and removes the last dependence on `lfunzeros`. Third, each run should emit a machine-checkable certificate: \(a_n\), the chosen truncations and the balls, recomputable by a small independent checker. That is the step from a certified computation to a proof-producing artifact.

Part VI. Closing the trust boundary

24. The budget, certified two ways

DerivedThe parallel session added two routes to the budget \(\mathfrak B_E=\operatorname{Re}\Lambda'/\Lambda(E,2)\). The first is direct, needing no GRH, rank or zeros: an Arb evaluation near \(\sigma=2\) with explicit derivative bounds. The second is a variational bracket from the moments. With \(a_j=\gamma_j^{-2}\) and \(d\nu=\sum_ja_j\delta_{a_j}\), one has \((\mathfrak B_E-r)/2=\int d\nu/(1+a)\). The pointwise inequality \(2q-(1+a)q^2\le(1+a)^{-1}\), which is \((1+a)(q-\tfrac1{1+a})^2\ge0\), optimised over polynomials of degree \(\le d\), gives \[ r+2v^{\top}G^{-1}v\ \le\ \mathfrak B_E\ \le\ r+2\big(p_1-w^{\top}K^{-1}w\big), \] with \(v_i=p_{i+1}\), \(G_{ij}=p_{i+j+1}+p_{i+j+2}\), \(w_i=p_{i+2}\) and \(K_{ij}=p_{i+j+2}+p_{i+j+3}\). I checked each step. The moments of \(\nu\) are \(\int a^kd\nu=p_{k+1}\). The upper bound is the same construction applied to \(\sum a^2/(1+a)\) with the measure \(a\,d\nu\). The bracket is classical moment theory and is correct.

MeasuredTheir generator had not been executed before, because their environment lacks PARI and Arb. I ran it here. Their default of 105 bits with 45 moments cannot succeed. \(p_{21}\approx\gamma_1^{-42}\approx10^{-34}\) lies below the working error, and the run stops with "\(p_{21}\) is not strictly positive". The bracket needs only \(p_1,\dots,p_7\), so I reran with 240 bits and 12 moments.

My exact evaluation sits at \(s=1\) of the Part V representation. Its \(s=-1\) branch is singular there, so I replaced it by closed forms. The value term is \(g_n(-1)=E_1(c)=-\gamma-\log c-\sum_{j\ge1}(-c)^j/(j!\,j)\). The derivative term is \(g_n'(-1)=\partial_a\Gamma(a,c)|_{a=0}-\log c\,E_1(c)\), with \(\partial_a\Gamma(0,c)=\tfrac{\gamma^2}2+\tfrac{\pi^2}{12}-\tfrac{(\log c)^2}2-\sum_{j\ge1}\tfrac{(-c)^j}{j!}\big(\tfrac{\log c}j-\tfrac1{j^2}\big)\). This algorithm shares nothing with the near-endpoint route except the coefficients \(a_n\). The two overlap on all five curves at widths around \(10^{-72}\). This replaces the Part II Euler-product budget, whose \(\pm4.1\cdot10^{-4}\) radius limited every comparison in Parts II–IV, by about 68 orders of magnitude. All the Part II values lie within their stated radius of the new ones. The variational brackets contain the direct values on every curve. Because the bracket assumes GRH and the stated rank and the direct value assumes neither, this agreement is consistent with those hypotheses, though it does not prove them. It holds even for 234446a1, whose rank is not provable. A wrong rank would shift the bracket by about 2 per unit of rank error and miss the direct value by orders of magnitude more than the bracket width.

25. Independent recomputation and a rational checker

MeasuredThe parallel checker rightly marked the Arb inputs as a trust boundary. I attacked that boundary from both sides. For the inputs: the Taylor coefficients \(\lambda_k\), which feed every moment, were recomputed by a different algorithm. That algorithm is rigorous Arb quadrature (acb.integral) of \(\lambda_k=\frac{1+w(-1)^k}{k!}\int_1^\infty F(y)(\log y)^k\,dy\), with \(F(y)=\sum a_ne^{-c_ny}\) and explicit \(n\)- and \(y\)-tail bounds. It shares nothing with the incomplete-gamma series of Part V. On 11a1, 37a1 and 389a1, 30 of 30 coefficients overlap, agreeing to about 40 digits. For the logic: every Part V result is now emitted as a certificate. Each certificate holds the node balls \(\mathscr H(t_j)\), the power-sum balls \(p_m\), the sign-evaluation balls \(Z(\tau_a)\) and \(Z(\tau_b)\), and, for completeness, every seed's sign balls. A checker of about 120 lines using only fractions.Fraction re-derives the following from them: the quadrature sum, the rational lower bound \(g\le\gamma_1\) via \(g^{2m}\,p_m^{\text{upper}}\le1\), a certified rational \(\rho\) via \((\rho-\mathrm{ch})^2\le\mathrm{ch}^2-1\), the error bound, the first-zero count \(p_m\tau_b^{2m}<2\), and the deflated remainder \(R_mT^{2m}<1\). All ten certificates validate, five for \(\mathfrak D_E\) with first-zero isolation and five for completeness. The checker rejects all six forgeries tried: a same-sign "zero", a count bound pushed past the second zero, a false \(\mathfrak D\) claim, an inflated height \(T\), a deleted zero, and a seed without a sign change.

26. The twist family on certified inputs

MeasuredI reran every quadratic twist of 11a1 with fundamental \(|d|\le60\) entirely on certified computations: 39 twists, conductors \(99\) to \(39\,600\), ranks 0 and 1. Each received a zero-free certified \(\mathfrak D_E\) (radii near \(10^{-35}\)), a certified first-zero isolation, and a certified complete zero list up to a height between \(2.64\) and the low 4s, median \(3.42\). The cut was placed half a unit above the fourth dataset zero, so the certified range always contains the first one to three zeros. The results are 39 of 39 on all three counts. The first zero was isolated every time. The certified \(\mathfrak D_E\) falls inside the Part III dataset bracket \([\mathfrak D^{\text{found}}+R,\ \mathfrak D^{\text{found}}+\sqrt{1+T_0^{-2}}R]\) every time. Every certified zero matches the dataset's PARI value to \(10^{-8}\). For this subfamily, the zero lists on which Parts III and IV were built are now verified, not assumed. The total cost was 36 minutes on 2 cores. Cost grows roughly linearly in \(|d|\), so certifying the full 492-twist family up to \(|d|=3000\) is on the order of days on this hardware. That is the honest price of making the Conjecture E test rigorous in all its inputs.

27. Status after Part VI

The spectral side of the Crest–Root calculus is now a proof-producing pipeline, with explicit and minimal trust assumptions. The heavy computation is Arb, cross-validated by a second independent algorithm at each analytic input: the budget by two routes, and the Taylor coefficients by series and by quadrature. The conclusions are carried by certificates that a short exact-rational checker validates and that it rejects when forged. Four things remain trusted and unchecked by the checker: the coefficients \(a_n\), conductor and root number, all from PARI; GRH, which interprets the zeros as real; and the rank hypothesis for 234446a1. Three things are now established at the level of certified computation: the budgets to 72 digits, the uncertainty functional \(\mathfrak D_E\) to 31–36 digits, and 101 certified simple zeros forming complete lists on the five curves, plus the low zeros of 39 twists. The natural continuation is to have the checker recompute the \(a_n\) from the Weierstrass model, by point counting for small \(n\) and multiplicativity, which removes the PARI dependence. After that comes the full-family certification needed to test Conjecture E with rigorous inputs.

Part VII. Removing PARI, and the arithmetic law on certified data

28. A PARI-free arithmetic checker

MeasuredPart VI left the coefficients \(a_n\), the conductor and the root number trusted from PARI. A dependency-free checker, written in pure Python integers, now recomputes all three from the Weierstrass model alone.

It first computes \(c_4\) and \(\Delta\) and factors \(\Delta\), by trial division up to \(10^6\) plus a deterministic Miller–Rabin test on the cofactor. It then requires every \(p\mid\Delta\) to satisfy \(p\nmid c_4\). That certifies multiplicative reduction, minimality at \(p\), and \(N=\operatorname{rad}\Delta\). It counts points: \(a_p=p+1-\#E(\F_p)\) via \((2y+h)^2=h^2+4f\) for odd \(p\), and directly for \(p=2\). This formula is correct at good, multiplicative and additive primes alike, provided the singular point is counted. It extends to all \(n\) by \(a_{p^{k+1}}=a_pa_{p^k}-p\,a_{p^{k-1}}\) at good \(p\), \(a_{p^k}=a_p^k\) at bad \(p\), and multiplicativity. It sets \(w=-\prod_{p\mid N}(-a_p)\). Finally it compares SHA-256 hashes of the exact sequences \(a_1,\dots,a_M\) against hashes committed by the Arb runs.

All five base curves pass for both truncations used (\(M\) up to \(12\,200\)), in 3.5 seconds. The conductors \(11, 37, 389, 5077\) and \(234446=2\cdot117223\) are re-derived, the root numbers \(+1,-1,+1,-1,+1\) are re-derived, and every committed \(a_n\) sequence is reproduced bit for bit. The twists are not semistable, so for them the checker recomputes \(a_n\) and, when \(\gcd(d,11)=1\), verifies \(N=11d^2\) and \(w=\chi_d(-11)\). That holds for all 122 hashes, and \(N\) and \(w\) match on all 111 twists where the formula applies. PARI is now only a fast generator whose output is independently re-derived. It is no longer part of the trusted base.

29. The twist family to \(|d|=200\), certified

MeasuredAll 122 quadratic twists of 11a1 with fundamental \(|d|\le200\) (conductors up to \(4.4\cdot10^5\)) were certified with the Part V machinery at 60 target bits and 12 moments, using 75 CPU-minutes. All 122 have a certified sign change at every seed zero. All 122 have a certified isolated first zero. All 122 have a zero-free certified \(\mathfrak D_E\) lying inside the Part III dataset bracket, and all 122 have certified zeros matching the dataset to \(10^{-8}\). The full 492-twist family was not certified. At \(N\approx10^8\) the coefficient count is \(M\approx95\,000\) even at 60 bits, and the Python-level alternating series costs about 20 minutes per twist. The whole family is about 40 CPU-hours here. That is a native-code (C/FLINT) task, not a mathematical obstacle.

30. The arithmetic law, without circularity

The parallel audit noted that the Part IV full residual borrowed its tail from the Euler-product budget, so its correlation with local Euler data was partly algebraic. The certified \(\mathfrak D_E\) is computed from \(\Lambda\) by quadrature without any budget, which removes that dependence. On the 113 certified twists with \(N>200\), at least three certified zeros, and a list complete through \(\gamma\le1\), I regressed the conductor-detrended residual on two small-prime predictors. One is my heuristic taper. The other is the parallel session's exact Euler weight, \(\mathcal P_p=-\log p\,(a_p^{(d)}/p^2-2/p^3)/(1-a_p^{(d)}/p^2+p^{-3})\), summed over good \(p\le P\).
