The exact Euler weights keep explaining most of it when extended to \(p\le47\), while my heuristic taper loses it. The parallel session's observation on uncertified data is thus confirmed on certified data. Signs agree with the monotonicity \(\partial\mathcal P_p/\partial a_p<0\). The \(\chi_d(2)\) ordering persists. At rank 0 the residual means are \(0.669, 0.747, 0.839\) and the first-gap means are \(1.443, 1.131, 0.976\), for \(\chi_d(2)=-1,0,+1\). The lowest zero itself is again flat across classes. Conjecture E remains untested. With 14 to 21 certified rank-0 twists per \(\chi_d(2)\) class, a conditional excised-ensemble fit has no power. The required sample, about 2000 per class, needs the native-code family certification above.

31. Status after Part VII

The trusted base of the spectral pipeline is now GRH (to read zeros as real ordinates) and, for 234446a1, its rank. Nothing else is trusted. Arithmetic inputs are re-derived by a PARI-free checker. Analytic inputs are computed in Arb and cross-validated by independent algorithms. Every conclusion is re-derived from serialized balls by an exact-rational checker that rejects forgeries. On this base, the certified statements are the following: budgets to 72 digits; \(\mathfrak D_E\) to 31–36 digits; complete simple zero lists on five curves; certified low zeros and \(\mathfrak D_E\) for 122 twists; and an arithmetic law, about 85% explained variance from three primes at rank 0, that holds on certified, non-circular data. Two items remain open. One is the native implementation needed for the full family and for Conjecture E. The other is a theoretical derivation of the exact-weight law: the explicit formula applied to the smooth part of the resolvent kernel should predict the coefficients in Table 12, not just their signs.

Part VIII. The full family, the law derived, and Conjecture E tested

32. A native calculator with deflated quadrature

The Python sweep cost about 20 minutes per twist at \(N\approx10^8\). The cost was in Python-level alternating series over about \(10^5\) coefficients. I rewrote the sweep in C against FLINT 3.0.1 (crest_native.c, about 150 lines). The mathematics, tail bounds and output balls are identical. The tables \(1/(1+j+s_i)\), \(1/(1+j+i\tau_i)\) and \(1/(1+j)^{k+1}\) are hoisted out of the coefficient loop, because they do not depend on \(n\). That leaves multiply-adds at each step. A second change is mathematical. Small \(\gamma_1\) forces the Bernstein parameter \(\rho\) toward 1 and the node count into the hundreds. So the quadrature is now deflated. With the certified complete list \(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_q\) in \((0,T]\), \[ \mathfrak D_E=\sum_{k\le q}\frac{2}{\gamma_k\sqrt{1+\gamma_k^2}}+\frac2\pi\int_0^1\frac{\widetilde{\mathscr H}(t)}{\sqrt{t(1-t)}}dt,\qquad \widetilde{\mathscr H}(t)=\mathscr H(t)-\sum_{k\le q}\frac1{t+\gamma_k^2}. \] Here \(\widetilde{\mathscr H}\) is analytic for \(\operatorname{Re}t>-T^2\), because the next zero exceeds \(T\). It is bounded on the ellipse by \(\frac{T^2+1}{T^2-a}\big(\mathscr H(t_1)-\sum_k(t_1+\gamma_k^2)^{-1}\big)\), which is exact because the list is complete. The node count drops to 6–12 even for the hardest twist (\(d=-2531\), \(\delta_1=0.065\)). The native code matches the Python results on 11a1 to 34 digits and on the twists \(d=-199\) and \(d=5\). It is 25 times faster at \(d=-199\), and it handles \(d=-2531\) (\(M=89\,485\)) in 94 seconds.

33. The whole 492-twist family, certified

MeasuredEvery twist in the Part III family (conductors \(99\) to \(9.89\cdot10^{7}\)) was certified at 40 target bits in 97 CPU-minutes. All 492 have a certified sign change at every seed zero. All 492 have a certified isolated first zero, and all 492 have a deflated zero-free \(\mathfrak D_E\) inside the Part III dataset bracket. All 492 have certified zeros matching the dataset's PARI values to \(10^{-8}\), and 483 have at least three certified zeros in a complete list. The zero data on which Parts III–IV rested is now certified throughout, apart from GRH. The earlier estimate of 40 CPU-hours for this run assumed the Python sweep. Native code plus deflation brought it down by a factor of about 25.

34. The arithmetic law, derived

DerivedThe kernels of the uncertainty functional and of the budget differ by an exactly computable, rapidly decaying kernel: \[ \mathfrak D_E=(\mathfrak B_E-r)+\mathcal E_E,\qquad \mathcal E_E=\sum_{\gamma\ne0}k(\gamma),\qquad k(\gamma)=\frac1{|\gamma|(1+\gamma^2)\big(\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}+|\gamma|\big)}\sim\frac1{2\gamma^4}. \] By Part VI, \(\mathfrak B_E=\tfrac12\log N-\log2\pi+\psi(2)+\sum_p\mathcal P_p\) is an absolutely convergent Euler sum. The parallel session's exact weights \(\mathcal P_p\) are therefore not an empirical choice. They are the prime terms of \(\mathfrak B_E\). For the residual after the first zero, \(Y=\mathfrak D_E-2/(\gamma_1\sqrt{1+\gamma_1^2})\), the identity reads \(Y=\big[\mathfrak B_E-r-\tfrac{2}{1+\gamma_1^2}\big]+\sum_{\gamma\ne0,\pm\gamma_1}k(\gamma)\). The arithmetic of the twist enters linearly through \(\mathfrak B_E\), with fixed relative weights \(\mathcal P_p\). It also enters through two zero-local terms that respond to the same arithmetic. The derivation therefore predicts the shape of the law: equal coefficients across primes when measured in units of \(\mathcal P_p\). It leaves the overall scale \(\kappa_r=1+\operatorname{Cov}(\text{zero-local},\mathfrak B)/\operatorname{Var}\mathfrak B\) to be measured.

MeasuredThe identity holds within certified bounds on all 122 twists where it was checked: \(\mathfrak D-(\mathfrak B-r)\) lies in \([\mathcal E^{\text{found}},\ \mathcal E^{\text{found}}+\frac{\mathfrak B-r-\sum_{\text{found}}2/(1+\gamma^2)}{2T^2}]\). On the full certified family, the budget explains 84.8% of the detrended variance of \(Y\) at rank 0 (\(n=200\)) and 76.0% at rank 1 (\(n=257\)). The predicted shape holds. Fitting separate coefficients for \(p=2,3,5,7,11,13\) in units of \(\mathcal P_p\), the equal-coefficient hypothesis is not rejected (\(F=1.06\), \(p=0.38\) at rank 0; \(F=1.82\), \(p=0.11\) at rank 1). The common coefficient is \(\kappa_0=1.93\) and \(\kappa_1=1.03\), matching the slope of \(Y\) on \(\mathfrak B\) (1.87 and 1.28). At rank 1, the prime coefficients enter almost exactly as the Euler factors dictate. At rank 0 they are amplified about twofold, because the zero-local terms move with the budget: a twist whose small primes lower \(\mathfrak B\) also pulls its second and later zeros toward the centre. Deriving \(\kappa_r\) itself requires the joint law of the low zeros and \(\mathfrak B\). That is a random-matrix question, which leads to the next section.

35. Conjecture E: the first class-conditional test

Current-edition correction. Historical correction: the original angular scaling was inverted. The corrected transform is θ=γL′/N, as reconciled in the subsequent sections.

Erratum (§38)This section uses the same inverted unfolding as §17. The corrected class-conditional test is in §38.

MeasuredWith 195 certified rank-0 twists (64, 76 and 55 in the classes \(\chi_d(2)=-1,0,+1\)), I fitted the two-parameter excised orthogonal ensemble separately within each class. The fit used a grid over the cutoff \(C\) and the effective-size ratio \(\lambda\), on \(\delta_1\) and the first gap, and the second gap and the low-lying residual were held out. The fitted cutoff increases monotonically with the class: \(C=0,1,2\) for \(\chi_d(2)=-1,0,+1\). Since \(a_2^{(d)}=-2\chi_d(2)\), the class with the most negative twisted \(a_2\) needs the strongest excision. That is the direction Conjecture E predicts, a cutoff shifted by the local data. But the class-conditional models do not pass the held-out tests. The second-gap KS distances are \(0.234\), \(0.121\) and \(0.217\) against approximate 5% critical values of \(0.170\), \(0.156\) and \(0.183\), so two of three classes reject. The low-lying residual rejects in the \(\chi_d(2)=0\) class (\(0.173\) against \(0.156\)). The pooled model rejects on the residual (\(0.188\) against \(0.097\)).

The verdict on Conjecture E as stated is that it is not supported. Conditioning on the local data does shift the excision cutoff, and in the predicted direction. But a two-parameter excised ensemble, even within an arithmetic class, does not reproduce the spacing beyond the first zero. Two caveats apply. The critical values ignore the fitting step and the simulation noise, so they are optimistic for the fitted statistics and roughly right for the held-out ones. And the matrix sizes are small integers. Section 34 points to the repair. The arithmetic enters the zero configuration linearly through \(\mathfrak B_E\), with weights \(\mathcal P_p\), and the excised ensemble has no channel for that. A model of Gonek–Hughes–Keating type is needed. In it, the arithmetic factor \(\prod_{p\le P}\) modifies the eigenvalue density itself, not only the cutoff. Its first testable prediction is that, conditioned on \(\mathfrak B_E\) rather than on \(\chi_d(2)\), the residual gap statistics should become class-independent.

36. Status after Part VIII

Four things are now settled. The certified calculator is native, deflated and fast enough for families: the full 492-twist family takes 97 minutes. The zero data of Parts III–IV is certified throughout. The arithmetic law has a derivation: its exact part is the Euler sum of the budget, which forces the per-prime shape, and the data confirm that shape. Conjecture E has had its first conditional test, which half-confirms it (the monotone cutoff shift) and half-refutes it (the held-out spacing).

Three open problems remain, and each is sharper than before. First, derive \(\kappa_r\), the rank-dependent amplification of the Euler shape, from the joint statistics of low zeros and the budget. Second, build and test the hybrid Euler-modified ensemble that §35 calls for, conditioning on \(\mathfrak B_E\). Third, extend the exact-rational certificate format and checker to the deflated native outputs, and run the PARI-free arithmetic checker on the large-conductor twists. That last item is a pure-Python point count up to \(M\approx9\cdot10^4\) per twist, and it should move into the native code as well.

Part IX. Every twist independently checkable

37. The parallel session's Part IX, checked

The parallel session supplied five things: an exact-rational checker for deflated spectral integration; an exact decomposition of the amplification \(\kappa_r\); a bound on the nonlinear correction; a correction to the unfolding used in the ensemble tests; and a hash-binding extension of the native code, which it could not compile. I checked each. With \(b(\gamma)=2/(1+\gamma^2)\), \(h(\gamma)=2/(\gamma\sqrt{1+\gamma^2})\), \(Y=\mathfrak D-h(\gamma_1)\) and \(A=\mathfrak B-r-b(\gamma_1)\), their identity is \(Y=A+\sum_{j\ge2}(h-b)(\gamma_j)\). It is the §34 identity restricted to the zeros after the first, so it is correct. Since the regression coefficient is linear, \(\kappa_r=\operatorname{Cov}(S_P,A)/\operatorname{Var}S_P+\operatorname{Cov}(S_P,\mathcal E)/\operatorname{Var}S_P\), and their split of \(\kappa_0=1.933\) into \(0.986+0.946\), and of \(\kappa_1=1.031\) into \(0.628+0.403\), is a correct accounting of what §34 left open. It is not yet a first-principles prediction. Their bound \(0\le\mathcal E\le(\sqrt{1+\gamma_2^{-2}}-1)A\) is correct. The ratio \(h/b=\sqrt{1+\gamma^{-2}}\) decreases in \(\gamma\), so every term with \(j\ge2\) satisfies \((h-b)(\gamma_j)\le(\sqrt{1+\gamma_2^{-2}}-1)\,b(\gamma_j)\), and summing gives the bound. The unfolding correction is also correct, and the error was mine: normalized ordinates \(\gamma L'/\pi\) must match normalized angles \(\theta N/\pi\), so \(\theta=\gamma L'/N\), not \(\gamma N/L'\). Their 17 unit tests pass here. Their checker passes the five base-curve certificates. Their C++ coefficient engine reproduces all 492 family hashes here in 4.5 seconds.

38. The full family under a three-link chain

MeasuredTheir hash-bound native source compiles here against FLINT 3.0.1. Its SHA-256 module passes their reference test. I reran the entire 492-twist family through it. Each run emits a complete certificate in their format (crest-deflated-rational-v1), containing: the 12 certified power sums, the six zero brackets as exact decimal rationals with their sign-evaluation balls, every resolvent node ball \(\mathscr H(t_j)\), the completeness height, the moment witness order, the node count, and the SHA-256 of the coefficient stream the native code actually consumed. The node count is now chosen for the checker's own conservative integer \(\rho\). The resulting chain has three links. First, the coefficient hash recorded by the analytic run equals the hash from the independent C++ point-counting engine, at the same truncation, for 492 of 492 twists, and it is identical across both native calls of each run. Second, the exact-rational checker, which bounds \(\pi\), the cosine nodes and the square roots in rationals, verifies the completeness deflation, the deflated quadrature and the error bound for 492 of 492. Third, every reconstructed enclosure of \(\mathfrak D_E\) has width at most \(8.1\cdot10^{-9}\) and overlaps the native claim. What each certificate still trusts is GRH, the analytic rank, and the Arb evaluation of the analytic input balls. The last of these has an independent second algorithm only on the base curves (§25). Generation took about 100 CPU-minutes, and the full audit took 19 minutes of pure-Python rational arithmetic.

39. The ensemble question, corrected

Erratum (§43)The PIT–KS values for \(R_1\) in this section used the plain transform \(P(X\le x)\). Because 37% of rank-0 twists have \(R_1=0\) exactly, that transform is not uniform even under a correct model. With the randomized transform, the untilted ensemble's \(R_1\) distance is \(0.18\)–\(0.19\), and the scalar tilt's is \(0.199\), not \(0.100\). The claim that the scalar tilt brought the residual near acceptance was an artifact. The two-sample KS values in Table 13 are unaffected.

MeasuredI redid the excised-ensemble comparison with the correct unfolding, sampling per twist so that each predictive draw is converted to ordinates with that twist's own \(L'\). The 200 rank-0 twists with \(N>200\) and at least three certified zeros were used. The fit is on \(\delta_1\) and the first gap. Held out are the second gap and the low-lying residual.

This replicates the parallel session's corrected result independently. The pooled second gap now passes, so my earlier claim that the pooled ensemble fails on it was an unfolding artifact. The low-lying residual still fails, and that failure is robust. Class-conditional fitting makes things worse, not better. In the \(\chi_d(2)=-1\) class, where the twisted \(a_2=+2\), even the fitted first gap is far off: the data's first gap is wider than any excised ensemble in the grid produces. The fitted cutoff still rises with the class (\(C=0.25,0.5,2\)).

MeasuredI then tested the parallel session's multiscale proposal in an out-of-sample form. For each twist, the certified resolvent values \(\mathscr H(t)\) at \(t\in\{0.35,0.6,0.95\}\) are interpolated from its certificate nodes with \(t\ge0.25\). That range is where the Euler product for \(L'/L(E,1+s)\) converges absolutely, so the values are arithmetic data, not low-zero data. They are centred within matrix-size bins. The excised ensemble is then exponentially tilted to match them, and each twist's own low-zero statistics are scored by their probability integral transforms under its tilted predictive distribution. A correct model gives uniform transforms. The untilted ensemble gives PIT–KS distances of \(0.079, 0.128, 0.084, 0.154\) for \(\delta_1\), gap\(_{12}\), gap\(_{23}\) and \(R_1\), against a critical value of \(0.096\). A scalar tilt at \(t=0.95\) gives \(0.120, 0.257, 0.063, 0.100\): the residual comes almost to acceptance, but the first-gap misfit doubles. The three-scale tilt fails outright. Its effective sample size collapses to a median of 2.8 out of about 30 000, and the constraint residual reaches 3.6. The large-\(t\) resolvent deviations come mostly from zeros above the spectral range of a matrix with 3–8 eigenvalues, so the constraints cannot be met. That diagnoses the obstruction exactly: any ensemble of fixed small size cannot carry the arithmetic that lives in the resolvent at moderate \(t\). A viable hybrid model must couple an Euler product, which carries the high zeros and moderate-\(t\) arithmetic, to a small random-matrix factor that carries the low zeros, as in Gonek–Hughes–Keating. A reweighting of the matrix factor alone will not do.

Conjecture Eis now refuted in every form tested: pooled, class-conditional, scalar-tilted and multiscale-tilted excised ensembles. Two observations survive it: the monotone shift of the excision cutoff with \(\chi_d(2)\), and the robust failure on the low-lying residual. Both point to the hybrid product model as the next object.

40. Status after Part IX

Every one of the 492 twists now carries a certificate whose arithmetic input is bound by hash to an independent coefficient engine, and whose deductions are re-derived by an exact-rational checker. The trust boundary is GRH, the analytic rank, and the Arb evaluation of the analytic input balls; the last of these has an independent second algorithm on the base curves only. The ensemble program has a sharp negative result and a precise diagnosis. The amplification \(\kappa_r\) has an exact decomposition, though not yet a predicted value. Two items remain. First, extend the independent quadrature recomputation of §25, which re-derives the Taylor coefficients, to the twist family, so that the analytic balls also get a second algorithm. Second, build the Gonek–Hughes–Keating hybrid with an excised matrix factor and test it with the PIT framework of §39.

Part X. Two independent certificate chains, and a model that predicts the residual

41. The parallel session's Part X, checked

Current-edition correction. Historical interpretation: the early Gaussian high-spectrum fit used inaccurate cubic interpolation and was subsequently withdrawn after certified exact-feature tests.

The parallel session contributed three things. First, a double-precision direct-integral cross-check of all 492 twists. After its own correction, it agrees with the archived values to better than \(5\cdot10^{-13}\), and to better than \(10^{-15}\) on 339 twists. As it says, about 18 digits cannot test the Arb radii. Second, a product-invariance remark. On the line \(\operatorname{Re}s=1\), a finite Euler product \(P_X(E,s)\) is finite and nonzero, so \(P_X Z_A\) has exactly the zeros of \(Z_A\). The remark is correct, and it is the cleanest statement of why multiplying in an arithmetic factor cannot move low zeros. Third, the Stieltjes inequalities for \(R_q(t)=\mathscr H(t)-\sum_{j\le q}(t+\gamma_j^2)^{-1}=\int_{\gamma_q^2}^\infty d\mu(u)/(t+u)\). These are correct as well: \(R_q\) decreases in \(t\), and for \(t_1>t_0\) the ratio \((u+t_0)/(u+t_1)\) increases in \(u\), giving \(R_q(t_1)\ge\frac{\gamma_q^2+t_0}{\gamma_q^2+t_1}R_q(t_0)\). Their arithmetic-dependent excision hybrid did not improve the held-out residual. Its PIT for \(R_1\) used the plain transform, which §43 shows is biased for this atomic statistic.

42. A second rigorous algorithm, and a second complete chain

MeasuredThe remaining trust gap was the analytic input balls, which had a second rigorous algorithm only on the base curves. crest_quad.c closes it. It evaluates the modular integral \(\Lambda(E,1+s)=\int_1^\infty F(y)(y^s+wy^{-s})\,dy\), with \(F(y)=\sum a_ne^{-c_ny}\), by panelled Gauss–Legendre quadrature in Arb. It shares nothing with the incomplete-gamma engine except the integer coefficients.

The construction is as follows. The panels are \([\alpha,\tfrac32\alpha]\), and each has a Bernstein ellipse with \(\rho=5.8\) contained in \(\operatorname{Re}y\ge\alpha/2\). The rigorous per-panel error is \(\tfrac{64}{15}hM_FB_k\rho^{-2n}/(\rho^2-1)\), with the majorant \(|F|\le2q/(1-q)^2\), where \(q=e^{-c_1\operatorname{Re}y}\) and \(|a_n|\le2n\), and explicit kernel bounds \(B_k\) on the ellipse. The truncated \(n\)-sum carries the tail bound \(2(n_0+2)q^{n_0+1}/(1-q)^2\). The range \(y>Y\) carries an explicit incomplete-gamma tail. Nodes and weights come from FLINT's rigorous Legendre roots. The theta values \(F(y)\) are shared by every kernel: \(\Lambda\), \(\Lambda'\), \(y^{i\tau}\) and \((\log y)^k\). So the engine is faster than the series engine: 1.4 seconds against 94 for \(d=-2531\).

On all 492 certificates, every power sum, every resolvent node and every zero-bracket evaluation from the quadrature engine overlaps the certificate's ball. All 1380 sign evaluations agree strictly. The total cost is 8.6 CPU-minutes. I then rebuilt every certificate from the quadrature balls alone and audited it with the exact-rational checker. All 492 pass, every reconstruction overlaps the original claim, and the widest \(\mathfrak D\) enclosure is \(8.1\cdot10^{-9}\). Each conclusion in the family therefore stands on two complete, independent certificate chains. The trusted base is now GRH, the analytic rank, and the shared ball-arithmetic library itself.

43. A conditional high-spectrum model, and a PIT correction

Withdrawn (§45)The positive result of this section depended on resolvent features obtained by cubic interpolation of certificate nodes. Certified exact values show interpolation errors with median \(0.026\) at \(t=0.35\). On exact features the full-rank model collapses (median ESS about 4), and its advantage disappears. The PIT randomization correction in this section stands.

Part X proposed separating the roles: a small matrix generates the low zeros, and a positive measure carries the high spectrum, with that measure constrained by the arithmetic. I implemented the simplest version. The low zeros come from the corrected-unfolding excised ensemble (\(\lambda=0.7\), \(C=0.5\)), with \(\gamma=\theta N/L'\). The high spectrum above \(\gamma_3\) is the smooth positive density \(\rho(\gamma)=(L'+\log\gamma)/\pi\), whose resolvent is \(\mathrm{ER}(t;\gamma_3)=\int_{\gamma_3}^\infty\rho(\gamma)\,d\gamma/(t+\gamma^2)\). The arithmetic input is each twist's certified resolvent at \(t\in\{0.35,0.6,0.95\}\), where the Euler product for \(L'/L(E,1+s)\) converges absolutely. For a candidate low triple, the discrepancy is \(e(t)=\mathscr H_{\text{arith}}(t)-\sum_{j\le3}(t+\gamma_j^2)^{-1}-\mathrm{ER}(t;\gamma_3)\). Candidates are weighted by \(\exp(-\tfrac12(e-\mu)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(e-\mu))\). The mean \(\mu\) and covariance \(\Sigma\), nine numbers, are estimated on training folds from the true certified zeros. Held-out twists are scored by PIT under 5-fold cross-validation.

One correction comes first. \(R_1\) has an atom at 0: in 74 of the 200 rank-0 twists, no second or third zero lies below \(\gamma=1\). The plain transform \(P(X\le x)\) is then not uniform even under a correct model. The randomized transform \(u=P(X<x)+V\,P(X=x)\), with \(V\) uniform on \([0,1]\), is required. With it:

MeasuredThe conditional high-spectrum model is the first model in the program to predict the low-lying residual out of sample. It passes \(R_1\) on all three seeds (the third at the threshold), and it passes the first gap on all three. Every ensemble-only model fails both. It does not yet pass everything. The median effective sample size is about 145, so the weights are informative without degenerating. Its success has a mechanism that matches §39. Arithmetic at moderate \(t\) is carried by the high spectrum, through a positive smooth completion, and the low zeros are selected by how well they reconcile the arithmetic resolvent with that completion. The matrix is no longer asked to impersonate the high zeros.

Conjecture F(Conditional low-zero law.) For quadratic twists of a fixed \(E/\Q\) at even root number, the joint law of the first three normalized zeros, given the arithmetic resolvent \(\mathscr H_E(t)\) on \(t\in[t_0,1]\) with \(t_0>1/4\), converges to an excised orthogonal law reweighted by a Gaussian likelihood. That likelihood measures the discrepancy between \(\mathscr H_E\) minus the low-zero resolvent, and the smooth positive high-spectrum resolvent \(\int_{\gamma_3}^\infty\rho\,d\gamma/(t+\gamma^2)\). Its covariance is a universal function of the symmetry type and the conductor scale. The decisive test is transfer: calibrate \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) on the twists of 11a1 and score, with no refitting, the twists of a different base curve such as 37a1 or 389a1. It is labelled a conjecture and not a result because, so far, it passes two of four statistics cleanly on one family.

44. Status after Part X

The certification program is complete for this family. Every conclusion about the 492 twists stands on two independent, fully audited certificate chains. Their coefficients are bound by hash to an independent point-counting engine, and their deductions are re-derived in exact rationals. The ensemble program has moved from a sequence of refutations to a first positive out-of-sample prediction, Conjecture F, with a clear transfer test. Three corrections in this part should be kept on record: the parallel session's unfolding fix (§37), the PIT tie randomization (§43), and the retraction of the scalar tilt's apparent \(R_1\) improvement (§39 erratum).

Part XI. Certified transfer, and the end of Conjecture F

45. The parallel session's Part XI, checked

The parallel session found that the §43 model was trained on interpolated features. It also reported that a frozen transfer to 37a1 fails on uncertified zero lists, and proposed a rank-2 truncation of the Gaussian precision. I extended the quadrature engine to evaluate \(\mathscr H(t)\) at explicit points and recomputed the three features exactly, as certified balls of radius below \(5\cdot10^{-16}\), for all 200 rank-0 twists of 11a1. The cubic interpolation of §43 was in error by a median of \(0.0257\), \(0.0168\) and \(0.0068\) at \(t=0.35, 0.6, 0.95\), with maxima of \(0.068\), \(0.042\) and \(0.014\). These errors dominate the two small eigen-directions of the discrepancy covariance. The interpolation noise had acted as an unintended regularizer, and the §43 result does not survive its removal. The finding is theirs and it is correct.

46. Two certified transfer families

MeasuredUsing the quadrature engine as the certification engine, I built certified families of quadratic twists of 37a1 and 389a1 for all fundamental \(|d|\le600\) coprime to the conductor with even root number. Rank 0 is certified directly by \(\Lambda(E_d,1)\ne0\), since the quadrature ball for \(\lambda_0\) excludes zero. That certification needs no rank hypothesis, so these families do not depend on the rank assumption the earlier sections carried. For 37a1, 155 of 183 even twists are certified rank 0. The other 28 have \(\Lambda(1)\) balls containing 0 and are excluded; they are presumably of analytic rank 2. For 389a1 the count is 146 of 185. The 37a1 count matches the parallel session's numerical selection exactly. Every certified twist carries a certified complete list of at least three zeros, exact resolvent features, and a Part IX-format certificate. All \(155+146\) certificates pass the exact-rational audit.

MeasuredThe certified central values give an independent certified test of the Waldspurger–Kohnen–Zagier structure \(L(E_d,1)\sqrt{|d|}=\kappa\,c_d^2\). In every class, \(v_d/\kappa\) is a perfect square to within \(4\cdot10^{-15}\). The classes are \(d>0\) and \(d<0\) for each of the three curves, with the 11a1 negative class split by \(11\mid d\) (additive reduction at 11) as the theory requires. The constants are: \(\kappa=6.34605\), \(2.91763\) (and \(1.75940\) when \(11\mid d\)) for 11a1; \(11.97383\) and \(4.90278\) for 37a1; \(19.92170\) and \(7.88695\) for 389a1. This covers 516 twists.

This reproduces the parallel session's Part XI findings on certified data, and it is decisive for the conjecture as stated. With exact features, the full-rank Gaussian law of Conjecture F concentrates on a handful of matrices and fails nearly every statistic, in sample and on transfer. Conjecture F in its stated, universal form is refuted. The rank-2 truncation is a fitted regularization, not part of the conjecture. So a curve-specific discreteness floor is part of what fails to transfer, and something else, probably the base curve's own low-lying arithmetic, is the rest. 48. Status after Part XI

Settled. The certified machinery now extends across curves: three twist families (11a1, 37a1, 389a1) with certified zeros, certified rank 0 for the new families, exact certified resolvent features, and rational-audited certificates. The Waldspurger–Kohnen–Zagier squareness is confirmed on all 516 certified central values. Conjecture F is refuted in its universal Gaussian form, and the §43 success is withdrawn as an interpolation artifact.

Open. The parallel session's positive-measure spectral-completion cone is untested. It conditions low zeros on the existence of a nonnegative high-spectrum measure, certified through the positive-semidefinite kernel \(K_{ij}=\int d\nu/((t_i+u)(t_j+u))\), and does not penalize a deviation from one smooth average. It is the natural successor. The cross-curve first-zero discrepancy, worst for the rank-2 base curve 389a1, now needs its own explanation.

Part XII. Spectral completion: from three points to many

49. The three-point theorem, checked

Theorem(Parallel session, Part XII; proof checked here.) Assume GRH. Let \(R(t)=\mathscr H_E(t)-\sum_{j\le3}(t+\gamma_j^2)^{-1}\), let \(U=\gamma_3^2\), and let \(t_1<t_2<t_3\). Put \(x=(R_1/R_2-1)/(t_2-t_1)\), \(y=(1-R_3/R_2)/(t_3-t_2)\), \(M=(U+t_1)^{-1}\) and \(c=t_3-t_1\). Then a nonnegative completion \(R(t)=\int_U^\infty d\nu(u)/(t+u)\) exists if and only if \(R_i>0\), \(0<x\le M\) and \(x/(1+cM)\le y\le x/(1+cx)\), with boundary cases realized by limits. The proof is short. With \(z=(t_1+u)^{-1}\in(0,M]\) and the probability measure \(\mu\propto d\nu/(t_2+u)\), one has \(x=\mathbb E_\mu z\) and \(y=\mathbb E_\mu\varphi(z)\), where \(\varphi(z)=z/(1+cz)\) is concave. Jensen gives the upper bound, the chord gives the lower bound, and two-point measures fill the region between them. Their audit reproduces here: all 501 certified triples pass, with the same minimum margin of \(6.99\cdot10^{-5}\). Their identity \(p_1=\Lambda''(1)/2\Lambda(1)\) is my \(\lambda_2/\lambda_0\), and their moment bounds on \(\gamma_1\) are those of §20.

50. The \(k\)-point obstruction and its resolution

DerivedFor \(k\) points the same change of variables gives a truncated Stieltjes problem. With \(t_{\mathrm{ref}}=\min t_i\), \(z=(t_{\mathrm{ref}}+u)^{-1}\in(0,M]\) and \(d_i=t_i-t_{\mathrm{ref}}\), we have \(R_i=\int\varphi_i\,d\mu\), where \(\varphi_i(z)=z/(1+d_iz)\) and \(\mu\ge0\). By Farkas' lemma, the proposed triple is impossible if and only if some \(\alpha\) gives \(P=\sum\alpha_i\varphi_i\ge0\) on \([0,M]\) together with \(\sum\alpha_iR_i<0\). I search for \(\alpha\) by linear programming on a \(z\)-grid, which is only a heuristic. Every certificate is then verified exactly. First, \(\alpha\) is rationalized. Second, \(Q(z)=\sum_i\alpha_i\prod_{j\ne i}(1+d_jz)\), which equals \(P(z)\prod_j(1+d_jz)/z\), has no root in \([0,M]\) by a Sturm count over \(\mathbb Q\), and \(Q(0)>0\). Third, \(\sum\alpha_iR_i<0\) at the worst endpoints of the certified \(R_i\) intervals. The certificates use exact certified \(\mathscr H\) at eight rational points \(t\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.35,0.5,0.6,0.75,0.95\}\) (squares of 45-digit decimals), computed by the quadrature engine for all 501 twists.

MeasuredNo true triple is refuted by either test, 0 of 501, as the theorem requires. On the parallel session's mismatched-triple benchmark, candidates taken from other twists at similar conductor scale, the two tests reject about the same share: 296, 292 and 286 of about 300 per family for three points, and 295, 288 and 284 for eight. The 8-point search occasionally misses a 3-point rejection. Mathematically it can only be stronger, because its point set contains the three, so the misses are failures of the LP search. The decisive difference is resolution. Perturbing one zero of the true triple by a relative amount \(\varepsilon\), the 8-point certificates refute at median \(\varepsilon=10^{-6}\) for \(\gamma_1\), \(10^{-4}\) to \(5.5\cdot10^{-4}\) for \(\gamma_2\), and \(10^{-2}\) to \(3\cdot10^{-2}\) for \(\gamma_3\), uniformly across all three families. The 3-point cone mostly cannot refute single-zero perturbations up to 3%. With eight resolvent values and positivity alone, the first two zeros are localized nearly as sharply as by the moment bounds. The third zero is constrained only weakly, because moving it mainly moves the support boundary \(U=\gamma_3^2\).

51. Status after Part XII

The spectral-completion line now has a complete positive-measure layer. It comprises the exact three-point characterization, an exact \(k\)-point Farkas certificate with Sturm verification, and a measured resolution showing that positivity on a few real resolvent values nearly determines \((\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\). Their point stands, though: a positive measure is not a spectrum. The next obstruction layer is quantization. The completing measure must be a sum of unit atoms at \(\gamma_j^2\), \(j\ge4\), and its counting function must obey an explicit Riemann–von Mangoldt bound. In \(z\)-space that becomes an integer-mass constraint on \(\mu\) near \(z=M\). Making it rigorous requires an explicit unconditional or GRH-conditional bound on \(S(T)\) for these \(L\)-functions, and that is the next concrete input to supply. Their observation that the 389a1 twists have lower central curvature \(p_1/L'^2\) (median 0.42 against 0.78 for 11a1 at matched conductor) relocates the cross-curve first-zero problem from statistics to arithmetic. \(p_1\) is a central-derivative invariant, computable before any zero is known.

Part XIII. Quantization, and zero counts without GRH

52. The quantization hierarchy, checked and reproduced

Theorem(Parallel session, Part XIII; proof checked here.) Let \(\nu\ge0\) on \([U,\infty)\) with \(\int d\nu/(t_0+u)<\infty\), and put \(\mathcal Q_\nu(z)=\exp\int\log(1+z/(t_0+u))\,d\nu(u)\). Then \(\nu\) is a locally finite sum of atoms with positive integer masses if and only if every Taylor coefficient of \(\mathcal Q_\nu\) is nonnegative. The proof is as follows. \(\mathcal Q_\nu\) is analytic on \([0,\infty)\). If its coefficients are nonnegative, Pringsheim's theorem places a singularity at the radius of convergence on the positive axis, so the radius is infinite and \(\mathcal Q_\nu\) is entire. Then \(\mathcal Q_\nu'/\mathcal Q_\nu=\int d\nu/(t_0+u+z)\) is meromorphic with integer residues, and Stieltjes inversion makes \(\nu\) the corresponding sum of integer atoms. The finite-order consequences are as stated in Part XIII. They are \(\mathcal E_k=\sum_{\pi}\prod_{B\in\pi}(-1)^{|B|-1}(|B|-1)!\,S_B\ge0\), with \(S_B=\sum_{i\in B}R(t_i)/\prod_{j\ne i}(t_j-t_i)\). For unit atoms, \(\mathcal E_k\) is a sum over distinct atoms of positive products.

MeasuredThe archive uploaded with Part XIII was byte-identical to the Part XII archive and contained none of the new code. So I reimplemented the hierarchy from the stated formulas, in exact rational interval arithmetic with partitions generated explicitly. On synthetic single atoms, integer masses 1, 2 and 3 pass \(\mathcal E_2\) through \(\mathcal E_6\). Mass \(\tfrac12\) first fails at order 2, \(\tfrac32\) at order 3 and \(\tfrac52\) at order 4, in the sign pattern of the falling factorial \(a(a-1)\cdots(a-k+1)\). On all 501 certified triples, using the 8-point grid of §50, every order from 2 to 6 is strictly positive. The smallest lower bounds run from \(0.0514\) at order 2 to \(8.19\cdot10^{-5}\) at order 6, against the parallel session's sixth-order value of \(8.21\cdot10^{-5}\).

53. Unconditional zero counts by Taylor-model contours

Every zero count in Parts V–XII rested on GRH, through the moment deflation. The argument principle removes that, but not by naive sampling. \(|\Lambda(E,1+i\tau)|\sim e^{-\pi\tau/2}\), while every majorant of \(\Lambda'\) stays \(O(1)\), so a Lipschitz-sampled contour would need on the order of \(10^{20}\) points at height 30. crest_taylor.c instead computes rigorous Taylor models. For complex centres \(c\), the coefficients \(A_k(c)=\int_1^\infty F(y)\frac{(\log y)^k}{k!}\big(y^c+w(-1)^ky^{-c}\big)\,dy\) of \(\Phi(c+x)=\Lambda(E,1+c+x)\) are computed by the panelled Gauss–Legendre quadrature of §42, with the complex kernel bound \(|y^{\pm c}|\le e^{|\operatorname{Re}c|L+|\operatorname{Im}c|\theta}\) on each ellipse. The remainder on \(|x|\le r\) is bounded by the positive majorant integral \(\int F_{|a|}(y)(y^{\operatorname{Re}c}+y^{-\operatorname{Re}c})\,y^{r}(r\log y)^{K+1}/(K+1)!\,dy\), with \(F_{|a|}=\sum|a_n|e^{-c_ny}\), evaluated by the same quadrature.

The certificate works on the rectangle \(|\operatorname{Re}s|\le0.6\), \(|\operatorname{Im}s|\le T\). It contains every zero of height below \(T\), because zeros of \(L(E,s)\) satisfy \(|\operatorname{Re}s|<\tfrac12\) unconditionally. The boundary is cut into pieces of length \(0.25\), each inside a Taylor disk of radius \(0.3\) with \(K=50\). On each piece, the samples satisfy \(|P_c(z_j)|>2(D_c\delta+\mathrm{Rem}_c)\), where \(D_c\) bounds \(|P_c'|\) on the disk. Then \(\Phi\ne0\) on the piece, and each ratio \(\Phi(z_{j+1})/\Phi(z_j)\) has a principal argument equal to the true increment. The winding number is a certified ball that must contain exactly one integer.

Three floating-point leaks appeared and were removed. Each one had made certified balls narrowly exclude their integer, which is how they were caught. First, circle closure: \(e^{2\pi i}\) in floats is not 1. Second, local coordinates \(z-c\) computed in float subtraction. Third, centres passed to the C engine as shortest round-trip decimals and not as the exact binary value, which produced junction mismatches growing with height. After the fixes, every winding ball contains its integer.

MeasuredA second certificate counts zeros in the disk \(|s|<0.5\), using one Taylor model at \(c=0\) valid on \(|x|\le0.6\). The windings are \(1,2,3,4\) for 37a1, 389a1, 5077a1 and 234446a1, each certified to better than \(10^{-26}\). The circle must lie inside the model's disk. A first run that violated this produced numbers that looked right but were not certified, and it was discarded.

What follows depends on the rank. For 11a1 (rank 0), \(\lambda_0\ne0\) excludes a central zero. The 30 counted zeros are therefore the 15 sign-certified critical-line zeros and their conjugates, each of odd multiplicity, so each is simple. That makes GRH true for \(L(\text{11a1},s)\) up to height \(27.76\) with the zero list complete, unconditionally. For 37a1 (rank 1), the root number forces odd central order and \(\lambda_1\ne0\) caps it at 1, so the same conclusion holds up to height \(32.74\). For ranks 2–4, the counts prove that every zero in the rectangle is either one of the \(2q\) simple critical-line zeros or one of exactly \(r\) zeros, with multiplicity, in \(|s|<0.5\). Numerical evaluation cannot distinguish a central zero of order \(r\) from \(r\) zeros clustered extremely close to the centre. That is precisely why proving \(L(E,1)=0\) for 389a1 needs modular symbols, and why 5077a1 needs Gross–Zagier. For 234446a1 no proof of central order 4 is known.

54. The twist families, now GRH-free in their low spectrum

MeasuredI ran the rectangle certificate up to each twist's completeness height on all 501 rank-0 twists of the three families. 491 certify at the default resolution. The other 10 fail only because a bottom-edge piece meets the critical line near a zero. They certify after refinement to pieces of \(0.1\) and \(r=0.15\). All 501 counts equal \(2q\) exactly. Rank 0 is certified by \(\Lambda(E_d,1)\ne0\). So for every twist, the certified low zeros are unconditionally all the zeros below \(T\), and they are simple and on the critical line. The zero data on which Parts IV–XII were built (first zeros, gaps, residuals, cone tests) is now free of GRH. GRH survives only where a statement concerns the spectrum above \(T\): the high-spectrum measure in the cone and quantization theorems, and the interpretation of \(\mathfrak D_E\) and of the budget identity as sums over all zeros.

55. Status after Part XIII

The hierarchy proposed in Part XIII is now realised at both ends. The middle layer, positive measure to quantized measure, has an exact characterization and a reproduced finite-order hierarchy. The final layer, validated zero counting, now exists: rigorous Taylor-model contours count zeros unconditionally. Those counts close the base curves up to heights 8–33 and every low spectrum in the three twist families. Two items remain. One is to raise the contour height on the base curves to the full range of the certified lists (28.6 for 11a1, 33.9 for 37a1) and beyond, which is cheap. The other is to combine contour counts with the quantization hierarchy on the high spectrum, testing \(\mathcal E_k\) on the remainder after removing all zeros proven below \(T\). That would put the cone and quantization statements on unconditional ground below \(T\), leaving GRH in force only above it.

56. Part XIV. The contour certificates raised to height 100

The rectangle certificate of §53 relied on zero lists certified by the moment deflation, whose completeness was itself conditional on GRH. native/contour_ext.py removes that dependence entirely. For a height \(T\) between two consecutive ordinates, it produces two certified facts from the same Taylor engine. The first is the winding number \(N_{\rm rect}(T)\) of \(\Phi(s)=\Lambda(E,1+s)\) around \(|\operatorname{Re}s|\le0.6\), \(|\operatorname{Im}s|\le T\). The second is \(q(T)\), the number of certified sign changes of the real function \(i^{-k}\Phi(i\tau)\) on \((0,T)\), with \(k=0\) for \(w=+1\) and \(k=1\) for \(w=-1\). Each sign is read from a Taylor model centred exactly on the line at a separating abscissa, as the ball \(A_0\pm\mathrm{Rem}\). PARI's ordinates choose the abscissae and enter nothing else. If \(N_{\rm rect}=2q+r_{\rm disk}\), with \(r_{\rm disk}\) the certified central disk count, then every zero with \(0<|\operatorname{Im}s|<T\) is on the critical line and simple. The cost of height is precision, not sampling. Since \(|\Phi|\) falls like \(e^{-\pi T/2}\), the coefficient object needs about \(2.3T+100\) bits and the working precision \(80\) more. I raised \(K\) to 70.

57. Quantization on the tail, after every proven zero is removed

Hadamard factorization and the parity \(\Phi(-s)=(-1)^r\Phi(s)\) give \(\Phi(s)=Cs^r\prod_{\gamma>0}(1+s^2/\gamma^2)\). So for any \(c\) with \(\Phi(c)\ne0\), unconditionally, \[\mathscr H(c^2)\;:=\;\frac{\Phi'(c)}{2c\,\Phi(c)}-\frac{r}{2c^2}\;=\;\sum_{\operatorname{Re}\gamma>0}\frac{1}{c^2+\gamma^2},\] summed over every noncentral zero \(s=i\gamma\) with multiplicity. The Taylor coefficients \(A_0,A_1\) carry their own quadrature and tail errors, so \(\Phi(c)\) and \(\Phi'(c)\) are rigorous balls with no remainder term. As a check, \(\mathscr H(1)\) for 11a1 agrees with PARI's \(\Lambda'/\Lambda\) at \(s=2\) to 25 digits, \(0.12654931083383525933742\ldots\). Each proven zero below \(T\) is enclosed to radius \(10^{-12}\) by two certified opposite signs of \(i^{-k}\Phi(i(\gamma_0\pm\delta))\), read from one Taylor model of radius \(0.01\). Then the tail \[R_T(t)=\mathscr H(t)-\sum_{j\le q}\frac1{t+\gamma_j^2}\] is a certified ball at every \(t=c^2\) with \(c\) real or purely imaginary and \(|t|<T^2\). For \(t>-T^2\) every tail term is analytic. Under GRH above \(T\), \(R_T\) is the Stieltjes transform of an integer-atom measure on \([T^2,\infty)\), so every \(\mathcal E_k\) of §52 must be nonnegative. A certified \(\mathcal E_k<0\) would place a violation above \(T\), with nothing assumed below.

MeasuredFor 11a1 with \(T=27.759\) and the 15 proven zeros removed, \(\mathcal E_1\) through \(\mathcal E_6\) are strictly positive on two six-point grids. The positive grid is \(t\in[17,624]\), and the negative grid is \(t\in[-767,-738]\), which is close to \(-T^2\). The sixth-order lower bounds are \(3.3\cdot10^{-9}\) and \(3.1\cdot10^{-7}\), each far above its ball radius.

Negative resultThe same certified values were then rerun with defects injected into the tail: the first tail zero at half mass, the first tail zero doubled, a zero below \(T\) wrongly left in, and an off-line quadruple at \(\sigma=\tfrac14\) in place of the first tail zero. All four still pass every order. At these probes the hierarchy is blind. The reason is structural. In \(\mathcal E_2=\sum_j m_j(m_j-1)x_{1j}x_{2j}+\sum_{j\ne l}m_jm_lx_{1j}x_{2l}\), with \(x_{ij}=1/(t_i+u_j)\), the cross terms are positive and come from infinitely many atoms. A fractional mass \(a\) on one atom turns \(\mathcal E_2\) negative only when its own \(x\) exceeds the sum of all the others by a factor of about \(2+2\sqrt2\). That requires \(t\) within about \(1/(2\gamma)\) of \(-u_1\).

It probes at \(s_i=T^*-\eta\{1.5,2,3,4,6,8\}\), so \(t_i=-s_i^2>-T^{*2}\), where the tail is analytic unconditionally. The calibrations reuse the certified \(R\) balls and alter only the first tail term. In the table, \(+\) is a certified positive \(\mathcal E_k\) and \(-\) a certified negative one, for \(k=2,\dots,6\).

CorrectionThis settles what §55 anticipated, and the answer is less than §55 hoped. Zeros of an entire function always have positive integer multiplicity. So on true data, the quantization hierarchy can fail only through an error in the bookkeeping: a phantom zero removed, a zero miscounted, or a defective evaluation of \(\mathscr H\). It cannot fail through arithmetic. An off-line quadruple is still a pair of integer atoms, only at complex positions, and it moves \(\mathcal E_k\) by a smooth small amount. The hierarchy is therefore a certificate that the decomposition is complete and consistent, with a calibrated sensitivity to mass errors at the first tail atom. It is not a test of GRH. The contour engine is the GRH instrument of this program. Combined with it, the cone and quantization statements of Parts XII–XIII stop needing GRH below \(T\), because the measure below \(T\) is now known exactly. But they gain no new arithmetic content from the combination. Above \(T\), they still describe a measure whose atoms GRH places on the real axis, and the hierarchy cannot see whether they are.

59. The parallel session's Spectral Foundry, checked

The parallel session proposed turning the program from inspecting objects into constructing them. Its first engine builds curves over \(\mathbb F_3\) and \(\mathbb Q\) as \((\mathbb Z/2)^r\) covers \(X:\;y_i^2=f_i(x)\), \(1\le i\le r\), of \(\mathbb P^1\), with pairwise coprime separable cubics \(f_i\). Every character of \((\mathbb Z/2)^r\) is defined over the base. So the Kani–Rosen decomposition gives \(J_X\sim\prod_{\emptyset\ne S}J_{C_S}\) with \(C_S:z^2=\prod_{i\in S}f_i\) and \(g_S=\lfloor(3|S|-1)/2\rfloor\). It follows that \(P_X(T)=\prod_SP_{C_S}(T)\), and by Riemann–Hurwitz with \(3r+1\) branch points (the roots and \(\infty\)), \(g_X=1+3(r-1)2^{r-2}\). For \(r=8\) the cubics are all 8 monic irreducible cubics over \(\mathbb F_3\), since \((27-3)/3=8\), and \(g_X=1345\). All of this is classical, as the parallel session says itself.

MeasuredI checked the receipts by two routes independent of the Foundry's C++ character-sum engine. The first is PARI's hyperellcharpoly, a different algorithm, run on all 15 sectors of the genus-37 cover and all 255 of the genus-1345 cover. Both products reproduce the stored zeta numerators coefficient for coefficient: degree 74 with SHA-256 fdf6caeb…, and degree 2690 with 46123be1…. The second is brute force over the fibres of \(x\). Over an affine point the fibre has \(\prod_i(1+\chi(f_i(x)))\) points, with a factor 1 where \(f_i(x)=0\). Over \(\infty\) all \(2^{r-1}\) points are rational, because each \(f_i\) has odd degree and the cubics are monic. The resulting counts \(\#X(\mathbb F_{3^n})\) agree with \(q^n+1-\sum\alpha^n\) for \(n\le6\) at genus 37 and \(n\le5\) at genus 1345. The values are \(24,56,48,152,104,920\) and \(128,896,128,2432,128\). The Foundry's own suite passes 7 tests in an isolated copy and skips 1, which needs a source archive that is not bundled. The recovered Part XIII suite passes 11.

60. Trace width bounds the group: a smoothness theorem

The Foundry reports a 686-digit Jacobian group order for the genus-1345 curve, and it warns, correctly, that a large order does not mean security. That warning can be made exact.

TheoremLet \(X/\mathbb F_q\) be a curve with an \(\mathbb F_q\)-isogeny \(J_X\sim\prod_iA_i\) and \(\dim A_i\le w\). Then every prime \(\ell\mid\#J_X(\mathbb F_q)\) satisfies \(\ell\le\max_i\#A_i(\mathbb F_q)\le(1+\sqrt q)^{2w}\). Given the factors, a discrete logarithm in \(J_X(\mathbb F_q)\) costs \(O\big(\sum_\ell e_\ell(\log\#J+\sqrt\ell)\big)\le O\big(g\log q\,(1+\sqrt q)^{w}\big)\) group operations. The proof is short. Isogenous abelian varieties over \(\mathbb F_q\) have equal point counts, so \(\#J_X(\mathbb F_q)=\prod_i\#A_i(\mathbb F_q)\). Each factor is at most \((1+\sqrt q)^{2\dim A_i}\) by Weil, and Pohlig–Hellman reduces the logarithm to the prime-order subgroups. The Foundry's trace width \(w\) therefore caps the discrete-logarithm cost at \((1+\sqrt q)^{w}\), independently of the genus.

MeasuredFactoring the 255 sector orders shows the bound is loose. The genus-1345 order, with 686 digits, is 829-smooth, with 17 distinct primes and \(v_2=956\), \(v_3=149\), \(v_5=92\). The largest prime comes from a genus-10 sector of order \(106112\). The genus-37 order, \(6796879185903206400000\), is 41-smooth. A discrete logarithm in the 686-digit group therefore needs on the order of \(\sqrt{829}\approx29\) operations per prime-power step. Low trace width is what makes these spectra computable, and the same property makes their groups useless for cryptography.

61. The inverse step with a global target: a genus-37 curve of rank at least 12

The Foundry's global example glues local choices at 3 and 5 by the Chinese remainder theorem. Its open problem is to impose global conditions, rank among them. For rank, the character decomposition already gives a handle. The action is defined over \(\mathbb Q\), so \(J_X\) is \(\mathbb Q\)-isogenous to the product of four elliptic curves \(E_i:y^2=f_i\), six genus-2, four genus-4 and one genus-5 Jacobian. Hence \(L(X,s)=\prod_SL(C_S,s)\) and \(\operatorname{rank}J_X(\mathbb Q)=\sum_S\operatorname{rank}J_{C_S}(\mathbb Q)\ge\sum_i\operatorname{rank}E_i(\mathbb Q)\).

MeasuredFor the Foundry's curve (3), the four elliptic sectors have conductors \(916=2^2\cdot229\), \(1832=2^3\cdot229\), \(196=2^2\cdot7^2\) and \(236=2^2\cdot59\). Their ranks are \(2,1,1,1\), each exact because the 2-descent lower and upper bounds of ellrank coincide. So \(\operatorname{rank}J_X(\mathbb Q)\ge5\) unconditionally, and the analytic ranks agree. The genus-2 sectors have odd conductor parts between \(2891\) and \(19455611\). genus2red leaves the exponent at 2 undetermined, so I record only the odd parts.

The local zeta functions at 3 and 5 depend only on the cubics modulo 15. So every lift \(f_i+15(k_2x^2+k_1x+k_0)\) keeps both prescribed Euler data, good reduction at 3 and 5, separability, and pairwise coprimality (coprimality mod 3 implies it over \(\mathbb Q\)). The CRT fibre is a free global parameter space, and in it the elliptic sectors decouple. I searched \(k_j\in\{-2,\dots,2\}\), giving 125 lifts per sector and 500 curves in all, maximizing the proven rank and breaking ties by height. The run took 5.3 seconds. The rank histograms in the box are, by sector, \(\{0{:}12,1{:}43,2{:}59,3{:}10,4{:}1\}\), \(\{0{:}38,1{:}61,2{:}26\}\), \(\{0{:}22,1{:}49,2{:}45,3{:}9\}\) and \(\{0{:}26,1{:}56,2{:}36,3{:}7\}\). The optimum is the smooth projective normalization of \[y_1^2=x^3+15x^2-34x+1,\quad y_2^2=x^3+10x^2-19x+4,\quad y_3^2=x^3+11x^2+3x-14,\quad y_4^2=x^3+11x^2-11x+16.\] This is a genus-37 curve over \(\mathbb Q\) with exactly the Foundry's local zeta polynomials at 3 and 5. All 15 sector L-polynomials at both primes were recomputed and are identical. Its elliptic sectors have conductors \(1578436\), \(33424\), \(247636\) and \(855832\), and proven ranks \(4,2,3,3\). So \(\operatorname{rank}J_X(\mathbb Q)\ge12\) unconditionally, against 5 before.

MeasuredThe certified central disk counts of §53, run on the four sectors, give windings \(4,2,3,3\) in \(|s-1|<\tfrac12\), each to better than \(10^{-26}\), with Taylor remainders below \(10^{-54}\). The analytic ranks agree. So every elliptic dimension of the constructed curve is BSD-consistent at the level the contour engine can certify: as many zeros near the centre as independent rational points. The remaining 33 dimensions are the genus-2, 4 and 5 sectors. Their ranks are not determined here, so 12 is a lower bound. By Faltings, \(X\) itself has only finitely many rational points.

This is the program's construction direction working end to end. Local spectra are prescribed at two primes, the global equation is realized, and a global arithmetic invariant is optimized in the CRT fibre. The result is certified by exact descent on one side and by validated L-function zeros on the other. The method generalizes without change to any finite set of primes and to any sector whose rank can be bounded by descent. What does not yet generalize is the step the parallel session named: discovering a decomposition when no symmetry is given in advance.

62. Status after Part XIV

Both items from §55 are done. The contour certificates now reach heights 40–100 on the five base curves. Ranks 0 and 1 have GRH and simplicity proven up to height 100, by a count that relies on nothing the program certified earlier. The quantization hierarchy has been run on the tail after complete removal of the proven spectrum. It passes, and calibration shows what it can detect. It catches every mass or bookkeeping error at the first tail atom and is blind to off-line zeros, so it certifies consistency, not GRH. The Foundry's decompositions are confirmed by two independent routes. Its trace width now has a theorem attached: trace width bounds smoothness and the discrete-logarithm cost. And the inverse construction has been extended to a global target, giving a genus-37 curve with prescribed local zeta functions at 3 and 5 and certified Mordell–Weil rank at least 12, BSD-consistent in every elliptic dimension.

The natural next steps follow from this. One is to push the contour engine to the twist families at heights near 50, which turns the GRH-free low spectra of §54 into GRH-free spectra in the statistically meaningful range. Another is to bound the genus-2 sector ranks by 2-descent on Jacobians, which can lift the bound of 12 toward the true rank. The third is to attempt the parallel session's open problem on a test case: recovering a hidden Kani–Rosen decomposition of a cover from its zeta polynomial alone, by factoring \(P_X\) over \(\mathbb Z\) and matching factors to candidate quotient curves.

63. Part XV. The parallel session's hidden-motive engine, checked

The parallel session's Part XV takes up the open problem of §62. It recovers a decomposition from zeta polynomials alone, without being told the symmetry. It builds rational Frobenius projectors from the factorization, and it runs a divisibility experiment over all 163 curves of the Foundry family. Its suite passes 12 of 12 tests in an isolated copy, and all 1,241 files of the Part XIV package are preserved byte for byte.

MeasuredEvery number was re-derived with PARI, from sector L-polynomials computed by hyperellcharpoly, with no Part XV code used (hm_check/verify_xv.py). The genus-37 numerator factors over \(\mathbb Z\) into nine irreducible factors of degrees \((2,2,2,4,4,6,6,8,8)\) with multiplicities \((6,5,6,1,2,1,1,1,1)\), summing to 74. No factor has a real root, so every Honda–Tate index is 1. The reading "three elliptic isogeny classes, six simple classes of dimensions 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4" is therefore correct. All 36 pairwise resultants have prime support exactly \(\{2,3\}\). The CRT idempotents \(e_i=(R/f_i)\,[(R/f_i)^{-1}\bmod f_i]\) in \(\mathbb Q[Z]/(R)\), with \(R\) the Frobenius radical, have common denominator exactly \(D_3=2^{18}3^{22}\). They are idempotents of \(\operatorname{End}^0(J_{\mathbb F_3})\) because Frobenius is semisimple (Tate), so \(R(\pi)=0\). Because \(\ell\nmid\operatorname{Res}(f_i,R/f_i)\) for \(\ell\ge5\), they lie in \(\mathbb Z_{(\ell)}[\pi]\) and split \(T_\ell J\) integrally, as claimed. The quotient \(P_{1345}/P_{37}\) is exact, of degree 2616, with leading coefficient \(3^{1308}\). The experiment gives 60 distinct spectra among the 163 curves (26, 19, 10, 4 and 1 by number of cubics) and 1,783 divisibility edges between consecutive genera, of which 512 are subset inclusions.

CorrectionTwo of Part XV's interpretations need adjusting. First, the genus-1345 quotient is not a hidden recovery. The genus-37 cover uses the cubics \(\{0,4,5,6\}\), a subset of the eight. The map that forgets \(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_7\) is a covering \(X_{1345}\to X_{37}\), and \(P_{37}\mid P_{1345}\) is its Kani–Rosen shadow: the identity of §59 restricted to a subset of sectors. Second, the "1,271 relationships not explained by the covering inclusions" are explained almost entirely, as §64 shows. They are not new arithmetic.

64. Why 163 constructions collapse to 60 spectra

The Foundry family carries a symmetry the experiment was never given. The affine automorphism \(\sigma:x\mapsto x+1\) of \(\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb F_3}\) permutes the eight monic irreducible cubics. It fixes the two Artin–Schreier cubics \(x^3-x\pm1\) and cycles the other six in two 3-cycles. It transports every equation of \(X_A\) to those of \(X_{\sigma A}\), so \(X_A\cong X_{\sigma A}\) and \(P_A=P_{\sigma A}\). It also gives \(P_A\mid P_B\) whenever \(\sigma^jA\subseteq B\). Burnside's count over \(\langle\sigma\rangle\) predicts \((70+4+4)/3=26\) orbits of 4-subsets, and \(20,10,4,1\) for sizes 5 through 8: 61 in all.

MeasuredThe spectrum is constant on every \(\sigma\)-orbit. The 61 orbits give the 60 spectra through exactly one accidental coincidence, between the orbits of \(\{0,1,2,3,7\}\) and \(\{0,1,2,5,7\}\) (hm_check/translation.py). Of the 1,783 edges, 1,352 are translated inclusions \(\sigma^jA\subseteq B\): 512 plain inclusions and 840 more. Every translated inclusion gives an edge, as it must. The remaining 431 edges are explained by no matching of sectors at all, since in each case the sectors of \(A\) cannot be mapped injectively onto sectors of \(B\) with equal L-polynomials.

The rest of the structure is visible at sector level. Every \(g\in PGL_2(\mathbb F_3)\) sends an irreducible cubic \(f\) to \(h=(cx+d)^3f\big(\tfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}\big)\), again irreducible, with leading coefficient \(\mathrm{lc}\ne0\) because \(f\) has no \(\mathbb F_3\)-root. For \(|S|\) even, \(\infty\) is unbranched and \((cx+d)^{3|S|}\) is a square. So \(C_{gS}\) is the twist of \(C_S\) by \(\prod\mathrm{lc}\), and \[L_{C_{gS}}(T)=L_{C_S}(\chi T),\qquad \chi=\Big(\frac{\prod_{i\in S}\mathrm{lc}_i}{3}\Big).\] For \(|S|\) odd, \(\infty\) is branched and only the affine \(g\) act, with the extra factor \(\big(\tfrac d3\big)^{|S|}\). In particular \(x\mapsto-x\) is a twist by \(-1\), a nonsquare, on odd sectors. It is an isomorphism on even sectors, a correspondence between sectors that does not extend to the covers.

MeasuredThe twist law holds for all \(24\times255\) pairs \((g,S)\) with no exception (hm_check/pgl.py). The 255 sectors fall into 64 L-classes. All but 6 of the classes are generated by this law, and the 6 remaining merges each join two genus-4 odd sectors, for example \(\{0,1,4\}\) and \(\{1,6,7\}\); they are accidental. The 431 factor-level edges have a counting explanation. All 255 sector L-polynomials are built from only 34 irreducible Frobenius factors over \(\mathbb F_3\): \(5,5,2,8,4,4,4,2\) in degrees \(2,4,\dots,14,20\). In degree 2 there are only 7 possible Weil polynomials \(1-aT+3T^2\), \(|a|\le3\). With an alphabet that small, divisibilities between products of many sectors are forced. They are real \(\mathbb F_3\)-isogeny factors, but they carry no geometric information and are not expected to persist at other primes.

DerivedThis sharpens Part XV's conclusion that a zeta function determines the isogeny category but not the geometry. In this family the lost information is the \(\langle\sigma\rangle\)-orbit, plus one accident. The \(\mathbb F_3\)-spectrum is a complete invariant of the cover up to the affine automorphism, with that single exception. The "excess" isogeny relations are the expected price of working over the smallest field with very few Weil polynomials, not hidden geometry.

65. Global correspondence synthesis, done for the family

Part XV proposes, without implementing, the search for global correspondences \(Z\) with \(Z\circ Z=Z\) that reduce to the local Frobenius projectors \(e_{p,i}\). For the \((\mathbb Z/2)^r\) covers over \(\mathbb Q\) the problem can be solved completely. The answer is a precise list of which local projectors lift and which cannot.

TheoremLet \(X/\mathbb Q\) be a \((\mathbb Z/2)^r\) cover as in §59, with sectors \(C_S\). Suppose that for every sector \(S\) of genus \(\ge2\) there is a good prime \(p\) with \(L_p(C_S,T)\) irreducible, and that for every pair \(S\ne S'\) there is a good prime with \(\gcd(L_p(C_S),L_p(C_{S'}))=1\). Then \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb Q}(J_X)=\prod_S\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb Q}(J_{C_S})\) is a product of division algebras. Its idempotents are exactly the \(2^{2^r-1}\) sums of the group idempotents \[e_S=2^{-r}\sum_{g\in(\mathbb Z/2)^r}\chi_S(g)\,[\Gamma_g],\] the projectors defined by the graphs of the automorphisms, with denominator \(2^r\). A local Frobenius projector \(e_{p,i}(\pi)\) is the reduction of a global correspondence-idempotent if and only if its block is a union of whole sectors. The proof is short. Irreducibility at one prime forbids a \(\mathbb Q\)-splitting of \(J_{C_S}\), since a splitting would factor \(L_p\) at every good \(p\). A nonzero \(\mathbb Q\)-homomorphism \(J_{C_S}\to J_{C_{S'}}\) would give a common isogeny factor, hence a common factor of \(L_p\), at every good \(p\). A product of division algebras has no idempotents other than sums of the unit idempotents. Reduction \(\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb F_p}\) is injective, and \(e_S\) reduces to the projector onto the sector-\(S\) block.

MeasuredBoth genus-37 curves satisfy the hypotheses: the Foundry curve (3) and the rank-12 curve of §61 (hm_check/global_synth.py). The witnesses use good primes below 20. All 15 sectors are \(\mathbb Q\)-simple, and all 105 pairs have \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}=0\). The largest witness prime is 13 for the Foundry curve and 19 for the rank-12 curve. So the global projector lattice of each curve is the Boolean algebra on the 15 atoms \(e_S\), with denominator 16.

Of Part XV's nine projectors at \(p=3\), exactly two are reductions of global correspondences: the two degree-8 factors, each of which is a whole genus-4 sector. The other seven provably lift to no idempotent in \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb Q}(J_X)\). The three elliptic factors of multiplicity 6, 5 and 6 each mix 4 to 6 different sectors. The degree-4 factor of multiplicity 2 mixes two genus-2 sectors. The remaining three each cut a \(\mathbb Q\)-simple sector into parts. At \(p=5\), 4 of the 10 local projectors lift.

The denominators make the same point. Each global projector has denominator 16, while the local projectors at 3 need \(2^{18}3^{22}\). Most of the local structure is an accident of reduction mod \(p\). The global structure is what survives every prime, and here it is visible already at two or three primes.

This also corrects the plan Part XV proposed. Searching for coefficients \(c_\alpha\) with \(\sum c_\alpha Z_\alpha\) reducing to a given \(e_{p,i}\) is, for seven of the nine projectors at 3, a search for an object that provably does not exist. The method that works runs in the other direction. Coprimality and irreducibility at a few good primes certify the global idempotent lattice first. Only then are explicit correspondences sought, and only for its atoms. Here the atoms come from the automorphism graphs. For a variety with no visible symmetry, the same certificate says exactly how many atoms exist and of what dimension, before any correspondence is found. That is the precise form in which local arithmetic constrains global cycles.

66. Status after Part XV

Part XV's computations are correct and reproduce exactly. Its two interpretive claims are refined. The genus-1345 quotient is a covering map, not a hidden recovery. The 1,271 extra relations are 840 translated inclusions under \(x\mapsto x+1\) and 431 factor-level coincidences forced by a 34-letter alphabet. The spectral collapse is the translation orbit, up to one accident. The proposed global synthesis is carried out for the covers over \(\mathbb Q\). It shows that the global idempotent lattice is certified by local coprimality at primes below 20, that its atoms are the automorphism projectors, and that most local Frobenius projectors cannot lift.

The next step this points to is a test of the certificate on a variety with no automorphisms. The certificate (irreducibility for simplicity, coprimality for \(\operatorname{Hom}=0\), and, when both fail persistently, a common factor at every prime as evidence of a correspondence) applies unchanged to a curve with no symmetry at all. A good test case is a genus-3 or genus-4 curve whose Jacobian is known to split over \(\mathbb Q\) without any automorphism, so that the predicted atoms can be checked against correspondences found independently.

67. Part XVI. The hidden-field test case, checked

The parallel session's Part XVI takes up the open problem of §66 with a curve that has no automorphisms. It is the plane quartic \(C:\;y^4=xy^3+2x^3+3y^2-4x-2y-1\), the member \(u=2\) of the family \(C_u:\;y^4=xy^3+ux^3+3y^2-2ux-uy-1\), taken from Laga and Shnidman. The family is tied to the real cubic field \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), \(\theta^3-3\theta+1=0\), which is \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_9)^+\) with conductor 9. Its suite passes 13 of 13 tests in an isolated copy, and all 1,276 earlier files are preserved.

MeasuredI counted points with a counter written in GP that shares no code with Part XVI (hf_check/counter.py). For each \(x\in\mathbb F_q\), the number of affine points is \(\deg\gcd(f_x(y),y^q-y)\). The projective closure has top form \(Y^3(Y-X)\), so it adds two points at infinity. Both are smooth: at \([1{:}0{:}0]\) the local equation has linear term \(-uZ\), and at \([1{:}1{:}0]\) it has linear term \(1\). Affine smoothness at each prime is certified by a Gröbner basis of \((F,F_x,F_y)\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) equal to \(\{1\}\). At \(p=19\) the counts are \(20,470,6863\), giving \(P_{19}=1+54T^2+T^3+1026T^4+6859T^6\) as corrected in Part XVI. The real Weil polynomial, defined by \(\chi_p(x)=x^3h_p(x+p/x)\), is \(h_{19}=X^3-3X+1\). The simplicity argument is sound: \(P_{19}\equiv\Phi_9\pmod2\), which is irreducible because 2 has order 6 modulo 9, and the leading coefficient \(19^3\) is odd. So \(P_{19}\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\operatorname{Jac}(C)\) is \(\mathbb Q\)-simple.

68. The split and inert laws

Part XVI observes that \(h_p\) is a \(K\)-norm at its four primes \(p\equiv\pm1\pmod9\), and that the test fails for three of four specializations at \(p=13\). It reads this as a field-of-definition phenomenon. That reading has a sharp consequence, and it can be tested.

TheoremLet \(A/\mathbb Q\) be an abelian threefold with \(\mathcal O_K\subset\operatorname{End}_K(A)\), where \(K/\mathbb Q\) is cyclic cubic and \(\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)\) acts on these endomorphisms through its action on \(K\). Let \(p\) be a prime of good reduction. (i) If \(p\) splits in \(K\), then \(h_p(X)=\operatorname{Norm}_{K/\mathbb Q}(X-t_p)\) with \(t_p\in\mathcal O_K\). (ii) If \(p\) is inert in \(K\), then \(\operatorname{tr}\pi_p=\operatorname{tr}\pi_p^2=0\). Equivalently \(P_p(T)=1+a_pT^3+p^3T^6\) and \(h_p=X^3-3pX+a_p\), and a curve \(C\) with \(\operatorname{Jac}C=A\) has \(\#C(\mathbb F_p)=p+1\) and \(\#C(\mathbb F_{p^2})=p^2+1\). The proof is as follows. \(V_\ell A\otimes\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell=\bigoplus_\iota V_\iota\) over the three embeddings \(\iota:K\to\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), each of dimension 2, and \(\pi_p\circ[k]=[\phi_p(k)]\circ\pi_p\) with \(\phi_p\) the Frobenius of \(p\) in \(\operatorname{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)\). If \(p\) splits, \(\pi_p\) preserves each \(V_\iota\), so its trace there is \(\iota(t_p)\). If \(p\) is inert, \(\pi_p\) permutes the three blocks cyclically. So \(\pi_p\) and \(\pi_p^2\) have trace zero, and the characteristic polynomial is \(\det(x^3-\pi_p^3\mid V_\iota)\), a polynomial in \(x^3\).

MeasuredFor \(u=2,3,4,5\) and every good prime \(5\le p\le47\), the zeta numerators were computed from counts over \(\mathbb F_p,\mathbb F_{p^2},\mathbb F_{p^3}\) (hf_check/laws.py). That is 50 good cases: 12 split and 38 inert. The cases \((u,p)=(4,5),(5,5)\) are bad. Every case obeys its law. At all 38 inert primes \(a_1=a_2=0\) exactly. At all 12 split primes, \(h_p\) is either irreducible and defines \(K\) (10 cases) or a perfect cube \((X-a)^3\) with \(t_p\in\mathbb Z\) (one case, \(u=3\), \(p=17\)). This explains Part XVI's observation at \(p=13\). There \(h_{13}=X^3-39X+a\) is a \(K\)-norm only when its discriminant happens to be a square, which occurs for \(u=2\) and not for \(u=3,4,5\). The other inert cubics define fields of discriminant 27297, 7224, 1101, … , or are reducible.

69. Where the endomorphisms live

Part XVI writes the new object as \(\eta\in\operatorname{End}^0(J)\) with \(f(\eta)=0\). Over \(\mathbb Q\) no such \(\eta\) exists, and this can be proved from point counts.

Theorem(Certified computation.) For \(u=2,3,4,5\): \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb Q}(\operatorname{Jac}C_u)=\mathbb Q\), and \(\operatorname{End}^0_K(\operatorname{Jac}C_u)\) is \(\mathbb Q\) or a field isomorphic to \(K\). The proof is as follows. If \(\chi_p\) is irreducible, then \(J_p\) is simple with Honda–Tate index 1 and \(\operatorname{End}^0(J_p)=\mathbb Q(\pi_p)\), a sextic CM field. Reduction is injective on endomorphisms, so \(\operatorname{End}^0_{\mathbb Q}(J)\) embeds into \(\mathbb Q(\pi_p)\) for every such \(p\). In particular it is commutative, and it is isomorphic to a subfield common to all the \(\mathbb Q(\pi_p)\). The same holds for \(\operatorname{End}^0_K(J)\), using only primes that split in \(K\), whose residue field is \(\mathbb F_p\). hf_check/endo_bound.py lists every subfield, via nfsubfields and polredabs, of \(\mathbb Q(\pi_p)\) at the 9 to 11 primes where \(\chi_p\) is irreducible. The only class common to all of them is \(\mathbb Q\). At the split primes alone the common classes are \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\mathbb Q[x]/(x^3-3x-1)\cong K\).

CorrectionSo the cubic structure Part XVI detected is not an endomorphism algebra of the Jacobian over \(\mathbb Q\). It is at most real multiplication defined over \(K\), with the Galois twist of §68, which is exactly why it is invisible over \(\mathbb Q\). This is the precise sense in which the Jacobian is "simple but structured". Over \(\mathbb Q\) it has only scalar endomorphisms. Over the cubic field \(K\) it can have, and by §70 does have, real multiplication by \(\mathcal O_K\).

70. The cover, checked, and the Frobenius element constructed

MeasuredThe identities for the genus-6 cover \(D:\;Y^9=r(x)\), \(r=\frac{x+1}{x-1}\big(\frac{x-3}{x+3}\big)^3\), all hold exactly (hf_check/cover_identities.py). They are \(r(-x)r(x)=1\), so \(\tau(x,Y)=(-x,Y^{-1})\) is an involution; \(w^2=z(v^2-4)\); \(Y^9+Y^{-9}=2T_9(v/2)=v^9-9v^7+27v^5-30v^3+9v\); and \(D(z)=(z-1)(z-9)^3\), with \(N(z)\) exactly as stated. Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus 6.

The step Part XVI leaves open, that \(D/\tau\) is birational to the quartic, I tested by point counts. Write \(D\) with its smooth model, with places over the branch points made explicit. Over \(x=\pm1\) the cover is totally ramified. Over \(x=3\), places correspond to cube roots of \(1/108\), and over \(x=-3\) to cube roots of \(-108\). Over \(\infty\), places correspond to \(\mu_9\). Then \[\#(D/\tau)(\mathbb F_q)=\tfrac12\big(\#D(\mathbb F_q)+\#\{P:\mathrm{Frob}_q P=\tau P\}\big),\] and both terms reduce to 9th-power tests in the cyclic groups of order \(q-1\) and \(q+1\). At nine primes, \(p=7,11,13,17,19,23,29,31,37\), split and inert, with \(n=1,2,3\), the 27 counts of \(D/\tau\) equal those of \(C\) exactly (hf_check/quotient_count.py). For a genus-3 curve these counts determine the zeta function, so \(\operatorname{Jac}(D/\tau)\sim\operatorname{Jac}(C)\) over each of these \(\mathbb F_p\) by Tate. This supports, but does not prove, the isogeny over \(\mathbb Q\). A Faltings–Serre bound or the explicit birational map would close it.

When \(p\equiv1\pmod9\), \(\sigma(x,Y)=(x,\zeta_9Y)\) is defined over \(\mathbb F_p\). The twisted counts \(N_k=\#\{P:\mathrm{Frob}_pP=\sigma^kP\}\) then give \(S_k=p+1-N_k=\sum_a\zeta^{-ka}\operatorname{Tr}(F\mid V_a)\) by Lefschetz, and hence the Frobenius trace on each character space \(V_a\subset H^1(D)\). The involution \(\tau\) swaps \(V_a\) and \(V_{-a}\), so \(\operatorname{Tr}(F\mid V_a)\) is the trace of Frobenius on the \(a\)-part of \(H^1(D/\tau)\). It is exactly the element \(t_p\in\mathcal O_K\) of §68, now read off the correspondence and not found by search (hf_check/frob_element.py).
